The Minister of Finance may, from time to .time, pay claims and accounts for ' work done or services performed ' upon the certificate of the chairman of the commissioners, when a sufficient appropriation has been made by parliament for that purpose. There is no reference here to the power to purchase supplies and materials, but that is plainly included in clause 2, which not only confirms the agreement, but authorizes and empowers His Majesty to do whatever is necessary in order to give full effect to it. A clear line of cleavage is drawn between the letting of work and the payment of ' work and services,' on the one hand, and the purchase of supplies and materials. The government has not divested itself of the power to purchase supplies and materials.
And the conclusion, after that long preamble-
Some horn. MEMBERS. Oh, oh.

If I were a lawyer, I would apologize for the length of it. But when I take a lawyer's opinion, and seek to communicate it to the lawyers in this House,
I suppose I must give the reasons for the opinion which I desire to submit. I liave seen longer opinions; but I like short ones myself.

You will feel that way still more when you come to pay the bill.
Some born. MEMBERS. Oh, oh.

If I have proved, as I think I have proved my original contention, 1 will gladly pay the bill, and save to this country and the manufacturers of this country, millions of dollars. This is the conclusion :
There is no reference in the contract to the construction of the eastern divsdon by contractors. That division Is to be constructed by the government, and no customs duties are to be charged by the government in respect of direct importations of supplies or material- whether for the original construction or for subsequent improvements or betterments. Economical construction being insured to the lessees by the agreement, the company is entitled to demand that the eastern division should be constructed as economically as possible, and the government could not, reasonably, or, in my opinion, legally, relieve itself from the obligation to import the supplies and material, if the effect of so doing would he to contribute to economical construction. As the Bill, in terms, confirms the agreement in all respects and provides that the eastern division .shall be constructed in the manner set forth in the agreement, it would appear to me to be a violation of the spirit and letter of that agreement to pretend that the delegation of the obligation of the government to its servants, the commissioners, in so far as the letting of contracts for the work is concerned, could have the effect of imposing a burden upon the company that, otherwise, it would not be hound to bear. The delegation of the ' charge, and control ' of the work of construction to commissioners. is a mere detail in the execution of the government's obligation to construct the-

eastern division

and to construct it as economically as possible.

Montreal. September 12, 1903.
Now, I think I will be absolved from the charge of making rash statements, of which I have been accused, when I say that in reading this Bill I came to the conclusion that clause 17 could only have one meaning, that it was put there for a purpose, and that purpose was to enable the government to admit, if it wished, all supplies used in the construction of this railway free of duty. It struck me that that would be a very serious blow to the manufacturing interests of Canada, and I contend that my contention has been justified by the opinions I have received. I do not think that my contention required these favourable opinions, because I think that any sensible business man reading that contract would come to the conclusion that that paragraph had been put in designedly for the purpose I have stated, namely, to enable the government, if they wished to do so, to import these materials and supplies free of duty. Further, if this agreement is carried out in its entirety, I believe the Grand Trunk Company can force the government to charge that company interest only upon the cost of construction of the road constructed in as cheap a manner as possible, and still be constructed efficiently. Therefore, it would be incumbent upon the government whether they built it themselves or let it out by contract through commissioners, to provide that wherever the material could he imported for the construction of that railway cheaper than it could be produced iu Canada, they were bound under that contract to import and to admit free of duty the material so used. Now, it seems to me there should be no question of that being allowed for a moment. This government are to construct a railway-we will assume that it will be as beneficial as our friends opposite profess to believe. They are leasing it to a large railway corporation at a rental, at a price on the' cost of construction, lower than has ever been known before. They are giving a great corporation a property costing $13.000,000, as the Prime Minister says it will, or $150,000,000, as most people believe. I say it will cost a great deal more than that before the 50 years are up.

Yes, if the expenditure goes on in the same manner as the expenditure on the Intercolonial has been going on, especially since our friends opposite came into power, if the capital expenditure goes on in the same ratio, and I see no indication of its ceasing, this transcontinental railway will reach the figure I have named, astounding though it seems to be. As I liave said, I do not propose to deal with the policy

of building this railway and handing it over to tlie Grand, Trunk Pacific, I am only criticising the contract whicli the government lias laid before us, and every clause in the contract I am entitled freely to discuss. Here is an enormous work, here is a work which will entail an expenditure by this country of $100,000,000. Now, I say that to cut our manufacturers out of the privilege of supplying these materials is to do a great injustice to them and to this country, because it is the country itself that has to pay for the cost. It is the country itself that will have to pay for the loss, if there be a loss, and I contend that in a ease like this, where the government are spending enormous sums of the people's money, provision should be made beyond the ordinary provision, and that as a rule all railway supplies and materials used In that road should be produced by Canadian manufacturers in this country. Even if it costs a little more, it will pay us in the long run. I am told, though I have not seen it myself, that tlie Australian government have advertised for tenders for a large number of locomotives for delivery commencing now and to last for several years to come, the condition of the contract being that these engines must be manufactured in Australia, giving employment to Australian workmen, no matter whether the locomotives will cost more or not. If you are to have manufacturers in your country you must first make a strong and stiff effort to begin them, even if you have to pay a little more at first. There is a great opportunity in this contract to establish railway manufacturing in this country, there is an opportunity which would realize what we all want to see, namely, the establishment of large rolling mills. Tjie extra cost perhaps would be less than the bounty that is now being paid on iron and steel if we insisted upon all these supplies being manufactured in this country. Other members of the Committee, I hope, will discuss these clauses very fully, because I feel perfectly sure that my contention, backed up as it is by the legal opinion I have quoted as to the meaning of this clause, is correct, and I say that the government ought to strike that clause out or amend it. Now, as the Prime Minister has taunted us with talking find not moving any amendments, I beg to move the following amendment to clause 1C :
Provided further that notwithstanding anything contained in section 17 of the said contract. any materials or supplies of any kind which are not the products of Canadian labour and which are imported for the purpose of the construction of the said eastern divison by cr on behalf of the said commissioners or by or on behalf of any contractors, workmen, agents or servants for the construction of the said eastern division, or for the improvement, replacement of structures or otherwise upon capital account for betterment for said eastern division as in the 16th clause of the said contract provided, shall be liable to the usual 355J
customs duties provided by the statutes in that behalf.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Committee is now discussing section 13.
We have been discussing section 16.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: No, section 13, and I call attention that this discussion Is out of order.

I am responsible for that. I asked that section 13 should be reconsidered, and that having been done and a satisfactory explanation having been given by the Minister of Justice, I thought we had passed it ; then we came to 16.
Section 13 agreed to.
Let us now take up clause 16.

My hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Osier) has already discussed the effect of this clause 16 of the contract, and I think he expressed at the time the Bill was under consideration for the second reading the opinion that he adheres to to-day. To-day. however, in corroboration of his opinion, he brings forward the opinions of two lawyers, Mr. Hell-mutli, formerly of London, Ont., but now of Toronto, and of Mr. Macmaster, of Montreal. Of course, it is almost impossible, listening to these opinions read hurriedly, to give any expression as to the value of them, and especially of the one we have just heard from Mr. Macmaster. It has been my good fortune to meet Mr. Hellmuth. 1 have had occasion to differ from him in regard to other things. It was my misfortune to differ from an expression of opinion be gave in tlie Supreme Court, and as to the result I will refer my hon. friend to the judgment of the Supreme Court in the case of the Calgary and Edmonton Railway.
That case lias not been decided yet. The Privy Council are still wrestling over their decision.
A reference was made to the Privy Council, but I think they disposed very speedily of the reference. It was all one way.
Lawyers will differ.

My hon. friend took tlie words ont of my mouth. These differences merely prove that lawyers like doctors agree to differ, and I am sure that my hon. friend got from these eminent counsel, Mr. Hellmuth especially, a man for whose opinion I have the very highest regard, the opinion exactly that he wanted.
I would be sorry to make that imputation against either of these two gentlemen.
Money will do anything.

I hardly wonder at that statement coming from the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Fraser). It explains a great many things. I am very sorry to hear the hon. Minister of Justice make the assertion that he has made as regards either of these two gentlemen that they would give an opinion in favour of my theory against their own legal opinion and against their own better knowledge and judgment. I may state that I have never seen Mr. Hellmuth on this matter. Mr. S. H. Blake sent the letter I wrote to Mr. Hellmuth. I have not seen Mr. Hellmuth or spoken to him. Neither did I see Mr. MacMaster before he gave his decision. I wrote to Mr. MacMaster from here asking him his opinion and I had not seen Mr. MacMaster or discussed the matter with him at all. I saw him yesterday on the train coming up from Montreal after I had received his opinion. If the hon. Minister of Justice, instead of making these assertions, will confute or contradict the arguments which have been given, I think he will be doing something very much more in keeping with the position that he occupies.
I am afraid that I cannot be bound by the construction put upon my statement by the hon. gentleman. I am bound by the statement I made and not by his construction.
Mr. Chairman

If my hon. friend will permit me. We must proceed regularly after all. In reference to the question that was put before and in regard to which the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) expressed his opiuion, I thought it would be proper for me to take the opinion of a gentleman who is responsible for the advice that is given to the Minister of Customs and upon whose advice the Minister of Customs must act. I had my own opinion on the subject, but I thought as this was a matter of the construction of the Customs Act it would be proper to consult the gentleman who under the law would be consulted by the Minister of Customs. I gave him Mr. Osier's speech to read and he gave me this opinion :
Mr. Osier, M.P., in his speech in the House of Commons on the 20th instant, quoted clause 17 of the contract .set forth in the schedule cf the Bill entitled: ' An Act respecting the construction of a National Transcontinental Railway.' See pages 9584 to 9586 of the ' Hansard.' He says that * i:t is a more serious clause affecting the interests of the country than anything else in the contract, that is that this is a case of the government building a railroad to cost at the least estimate $80,000,000 and that the whole of the materials used in the construction of the road shall come into the country at all times free of duty. He says that under this contract we bring in steel rails and everything to be used in the construction of the railway free, and that if the contract is Mr. 06LER.
to be carried out there will not be a steel rail roiled in Canada for fifty years. Again he says ' according to this contract, the fovernment, if they construct this road themselves, or through contractors, or under the supervision of commissions, are to bring everything free of duty.'
Mr. Newcombe, the Deputy Minister of Justice, wbo gave the opinion that I am about to quote, had nothing to do with the drawing of this contract. He was out of the country at the time the contract was made. This is the opinion that Mr. Newcombe gave :
It is impossible for me to conceive how such observations could have been made by any person who had carefully read and considered the provisions of the Bill and contract affecting this point, and given due value to the words used.
That is Mr. Neweombe's opiniou and as I have bad occasion to say before in this House, not only because of the position he occupies, not only because of the experience he has had in connection with the construction of the Customs Act, but because of his standing at the Bar, I am quite satisfied to rely on his opinion. Now, I venture to give my own opinion with ail due deference-
Is that all of Mr. Newcombe's opinion ?
I will give you my own opinion in which Mr. Newcombe concurs.
Did Mr. Newcombe give any further opinion ?

Clause 17 of the contract depends upon the preceding one. Clauses 16 and 17 are as follows :
In case, after the completion of the said eastern division and the .taking possession thereof by the company under the lease thereof, hereinafter referred to, or at any time thereafter during the continuance of the said lease, the government should deem it necessary to expend any sums of money for the improvement cf the said eastern division, the replacement of structures by others more modern, or otherwise upon capital account for betterments, and not being * working expenditure ' payable by the company, the government may expend such sums, and the amount thereof shall be added to the capital of the construction account at the end "of the year in which such expenditure takes place, and shall thereafter be considered as part of the cost of construction, upon which interest, by way of rental, is to be paid by the company ; provided that no such expenditure shall he entered upon without the consent and approval of the said company.
No addition shall be made to the cost of construction or to the capital of construction account in respect of customs duties in cases where there is direct importation of materia! or supplies by the government.
Clause 15 of the contract defines the expression ' cost of construction.' Clauses 16 and 17 provide for addition to the cost of construction. It is imperative under the Bill that the work of construction of the eastern section shall be by contract, and the Bill does not enable the

government to import or pay for materials to be U3ed in construction. Those, as I understand the Bill, are to be furnished bv contractor. Consequently clauses 16 and 17 of the contract can have no application to original construction. They apply after the completion of the eastern division and lease .of it to the company, and they authorize the government with the consent .and approval of .the company to expend money upon the eastern division for its improvement and betterment which amounts is to be added to the cost of construction as ascertained under clause 15 of the contract, but if in these improvements and betterments the government imports materials direct, the addition to the host of construction authorized by clause 16 is not to include any customs duties.
Sections 15 and 16 of the Bill require the commissioners to construct the eastern division by contract. There is, however, no provision requiring the work of improvement and betterment referred to in clause 16 of the contract to he done by contractors. The government may if they see fit carry out these works themselves, and if so, and in so far as they use material imported direct by the government they are not to charge any customs duties on the addition which is to be made to the cost of construction. This, I have no doubt,
the legal effect of the clause so far as the point in question is concerned.
That Is my conclusion, a conclusion in which Mr. Newcombe concurs.
At one o'clock, House took recess.
Committee resumed at three o'clock.
On section 16,
Mr. BORDEN iHalifax). It is to be greatly regretted that the Minister of Justice should have taken the attitude, with regard to the legal gentleman whose opinions were quoted by the hon. gentleman from Toronto (Mr. Osier), that he has seen fit to express to the House. The Minister of Justice did not express himself in quite so brutal a manner as tlie hon, member for Guysborougli (Mr. Fraser), but his intention was evidently the same, namely, to suggest to the House that the opinion of these legal gentlemen could not he relied upon, because they would expect a fee.

The fact that my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) makes that statement would lead me to suppose that my words were capable of being construed in such a way. I entirely disavow the intention of conveying that meaning. If such a construction could possibly be put on my words. I withdraw them.
The member from Guys-borough should withdraw too.

That is what I would have expected from the Minister of Justice, but I am bound to say that in view of the emphasis which he placed on his words, I gathered from them exactly the same impression as they evidently conveyed to the member for Guysborougii. I trust and believe that reputable members of the
Bar in Canada are not so lost to the sense of duty which they owe to the profession and to themselves, as to be influenced in the giving of legal opinions by what may be considered as the desire of those who seek these opinions. My bon. friend (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) also referred to the opinion of the Deputy Minister of Justice, for whose standing at the Bar and for whose ability I entertain the very highest possible respect; but I venture to think that the well-considered opinions read by my hon. friend (Mr. Osier) deserve a little better answer than the reply, even from the Deputy Minister of Justice, that he cannot conceive how any one could entertain such an opinion. There is no one at the Bar for whose opinion I would entertain a higher respect than for that of my friend the Deputy Minister of justice, but even what amounted almost to a sneer from him, is no answer to the opinions that have been read in the House to-day. I do not know that I sufficiently followed the opinion of the Minister of Justice to be able to criticise it, but perhaps he will be good enough to send over a copy to me. I agree with him that it is absolutely impossible, upon first hearing read an opinion upon a difficult legal point, to express a very safe conclusion as to whether that opinion is sound or not. However, I followed as well as I could the opinions read by my bon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Osier) and also the opinion read by the Minister of Justice, and it does seem to me that this is not a question that can be lightly dismissed by the government. In the first place, you have certain clauses of the contract which have been adverted to in the opinions which have been read. You have clause 5, of the contract, which provides (I omit unnecessary words) :
The said eastern division shall be constructed by and at the expense of the government.
Then you have clause 7 of the contract, in which it is provided :
In order to insure, for the protection of the company as lessees of the eastern division of the said railway, the economical construction thereof in such a manner that it can be operated to the best advantage, it is hereby agreed that the specifications for the construction of the eastern division shall be submlted to, and approved of by, the company before the commencement of the work, and that the said work shall be done according to the said specifications and shall be subject to the joint supervision, inspection and acceptance of the chief engineer appointed by the government and the chief engineer of the company, and in the event of differences as to the specifications, or in case the said engineers shall differ as to the work, the questions in dispute shall be determined by the said engineers and a third arbitrator, to be chosen in the manner provided in paragraph four of this agreement. '
Then you have paragraph 16, which in short provides that certain additions to the capital account may be made during the

period of the lease and the concluding words of that paragraph are :
Provided that no such expenditure shall be entered upon without the consent and approval of the said company.
Then follows clause 17, to which attention has been principally directed :
No addition shall be made to the cost of construction or to the capital of construction account in respect to customs duties in cases where there is direct importation of material or supplies by the government.
Now the argument of the gentlemen whose opinions have been read to the House is, that the government having undertaken to construct the eastern division of this railway, and having covenanted that no addition shall be made to the cost of construction in respect to customs duties in cases where there is direct importation of material or supplies by the government; that under those circumstances the government is not able to relieve itself from that stipulation or condition by reason of the fact that it entrusts the construction of this railway to contractors. It seems to me that that is a pretty serious question for the consideration of the Minister of Justice. On a previous occasion, he expressed himself to the effect that the provisions of the contract which might operate in the way I have mentioned, were overridden in some way by the provisions of the Bill. Let us look at the provisions of the Bill and see whether there is anything that operates in that way. Section 8 of the Bill referring to the provisions of the contract provides :
The eastern division of the said Transcontinental Railway extending from the city of Moncton to the city of Winnipeg, shall be constructed by or for the government in the manner hereinafter provided 'and subject to the terms and provisions of the said agreement of the 29th July. 1903.
Section 9 provides :
The construction of the said eastern division and its management until completed and leased to the said company pursuant to the provisions of the said agreement shall be under the charge and control of three commissioners, to be appointed by the Governor in Council, who shall hold office during pleasure, and who, and their successors in office, shall be a body corporate under the name of ' The Commissioners of the Transcontinental Railway ' and are hereinafter called * the commissioners.'
These commissioners are merely a body of servants employed by the government at pleasure, and they are to have control of the construction of the eastern division. Section 15, to which the Minister of Justice referred this morning says :
The said commissioners shall have in respect .to the said eastern division, in addition to all the rights and powers conferred by this Act, ail the rights, powers, remedies and immunities conferred upon a railway company under the Railway Act and amendments thereto, &c., &c.
Is it possible that there is any answer to the argument in the two opinions that have been read, that the government cannot free itself from the stipulation or provision which is contained in the contract, merely by reason of the fact that it employs commissioners, and through these commissioners engages contractors to do the work which the government has bound itself by the terms of this agreement to do ? Is there anything in the contract which would justify a conclusion of that kind ? Is it not a controlling feature of this contract, that the cost of that railway shall not be increased by means of customs duties upon material imported into Canada expressly for the construction of that railway ? That is what the contract would seem to intend, and how is the government to relieve itself from that feature of the contract by employing commissioners ? Suppose the commissioners, acting merely as servants of the government or agents of the government, construct tills eastern division by day's labour, and if these commissioners, who are capable of being dismissed at a moment's notice by the government, should import material which must be paid for by the government for the construction of this railway ; would you say in such a case that the government could escape the effect of this stipulation ? Let us take another illustration. Suppose we have two corporations, one undertaking to build this railway for another corporation, and that the contracting corporation should undertake to build it by day's work, and should undertake that the cost of material should not be increased by reason of any customs duties upon material imported directly for that railway ; could the corporation so contracting relieve itself from liability in that regard by handing the work over to a subcontractor ? I would venture to think that there would be at least a great deal of doubt about that. As I have said, I have not been able to follow sufficiently the opinion of the Minister of Justice, in which he seeks to establish'the conclusion that the government would be so relieved from this stipulation. I would be glad if the Minister of Justice would do me the courtesy to submit the opinion which he has read to the House, and which possibly might have the effect of modifying the opinion which X at present entertain.
I am having a copy made, and my hon. friend shall have it in five or ten minutes.

On the legal question which has been raised, I do not presume to offer any opinion ; that will have to be left to my friends of the legal profession. But I submit that the main question involved in this discussion is not the legal question at all. The legal opinions which my hon. friend from Toronto has obtained at such great length do not touch

the question which he brought before this House. The question which my hon. friend brought before this House was not a legal question, but an industrial one-the question whether or not the goods imported by contractors for the building of this road would or would not be subject to customs duties. That is not a question of law, but is in a sense a question of fact-an industrial question. We have dealt with that question fully, fairly and squarely, so that there is no room for doubt or debate upon it. We say on behalf of the government that every dollar's worth of goods imported by any contractor for the purposes of this contract will be made to pay duty at the customs house in Canada. We have said that again and again. My hon. friend said the contrary. He even went so far as to say that under this contract not a rail would would be rolled in Canada for fifty years. We state as a matter of intention on behalf of the government
Why not put it in the law ?
In the first place, we are advised that it is in the law.
It is a matter of contract.

It is not a matter of contract. My hon. friend from Toronto has had no legal opinion which says that that is a matter of contract at all. He has obtained a legal opinion on an entirely different, matter. The main question is an industrial one; the people of Canada who are interested in the manufacture of goods of various kinds desire to know whether the goods imported for the construction of this railway will have to pay the ordinary customs duties ? We say they will.
Does the hon. minister say further that the Grand Trunk Company under this contract, would be forced to pay three per cent on the amount of those duties V

That is another question. I want first to deal with the main question-the industrial question. After all the question raised by my hon. friend from Toronto was with regard to the industries of Canada. The question was whether goods imported by contractors for the construction of this railway, if they have to be imported, will be subject to the ordinary customs duties. I say on behalf of myself as Minister of Finance, having something to do with the fiscal policy of the country, that every dollar's worth of these goods will have to pay duty ; I say it in my capacity as acting Minister of Railways and Canals, having something to do with the contract ; I say it on behalf of the Minister of Customs, who has to do with the ad
ministration of the customs law ; I say, on behalf of the government generally, that every penny's worth of goods imported by any contractor for the construction of this road must pay the ordinary customs duties. There is no room for doubt or dispute as to that. But my hon. friend has submitted to his legal friends in Toronto an entirely different question, one with -which the industrial element of Canada has no concern whatever. He has submitted to them the question whether on the completion of this road and the adjustment of the capital account, we shall be able to include in the capital account the duties which will have been paid on the goods imported for the construction of the road. We are advised that we can include those duties. I do not wish to dwell on that, because it may be a legal question. But that does not affect the other question at all. We shall collect the duties at the customs house, and whatever advantage there may be to the industries of Canada, they will have received that advantage. Whether or not in the final adjustment with the Grand Trunk Pacific Company we may be able to charge them interest on those duties, is a question of law which does not in any way touch the industrial question. On the question whether these goods shall pay duty or not, my hon. friend from Toronto has no legal opinion at all. There is not a line in what he has read which says that these goods shall be free from duty. The whole argument of his legal friends deals with the adjustment of the capital account after the completion of the road ; and his argument goes to claim that we shall not be able to charge the Grand Trunk Pacific Company interest upon the duties which have been so exacted, That is a legal question. We are advised against the views presented by the legal adviser of my hon. friend. But I do not wish to discuss that question at all. I am confining myself to the industrial question, and I say that he has no legal opinion at variance in the slightest degree with the view taken by the government, that every dollar's worth of goods imported must pay duty. So that the^ people interested in the industries of Canada will have the advantage of that fact, and they have no more concern than any other people in the ultimate adjustment of the capital account.
My hon. friend the Minister of Finance is taking a rather remarkable position with regard to this subject.
Very effective.

My hon. friend the Minister of Finance may at least congratulate himself upon the fact that he has the support of the hon. member for Guysborougb. My hon. friend says he will not dwell on the question whether or not the rental to be paid by the Grand Trunk

Pacific shall include three per cent on the amount of the customs duties, a very pertinent question as to which was put to him by my hon. friend from East York.
Not the industrial question.
I do not know what my hon. friend thinks we are discussing. I supposed that we were discussing the terms of this Bill, and whether it was a good thing or a bad thing for the country.
I was discussing a point raised by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier), confining myself to that point, and not dealing with the whole Bill.

The argument of my hon. friend from Toronto touches the point which I am now bringing to the attention of the House. The hon. minister says he will not dvsell on the question" whether three per cent interest will be charged on the amount of the duties on those goods. The value of the goods imported will be at least, I suppose, $10,000,000 or $12,000,000, on which three per cent interest will amount to $300,000 or $350,000 a year. The hon. minister says he will not dwell on that question

I did not say that.
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax), -and wheii two opinions by eminent legal gentlemen are brought before the House by the hon. member for West Toronto, my hon. friend the Minister of Finance says they do not at all touch the question we are discussing. I think they do most closely, and I think it is somewhat important to this House to know, before we go through that clause 16, whether or not the Grand Trunk Pacific Company shall escape the payment of $300,000 or $350,000 per annum of rental for a period of some fifty years-a sum which in the aggregate would amount to some $15,000,000 for the whole period of this lease. So far as the industrial question is concerned, my hon. friend the Minister of Finance says he can assure this House of a certain condition of affairs. I do not suppose my hon. friend is above the law. I suppose that if the law should say that those duties are not payable, my hon. friend, in the absence of legislation, would not be very well able to control that matter, and if the courts held that goods imported by commissioners appointed under the provisions of section 9 were really goods imported by the government within the meaning of the statute to which my hon. friend from Toronto referred, I suppose the government would have to be bound by the decision of the eourt to that effect. Even if my hon. friend the Minister of Finance went into the court and gave to it the assurance which he has given to the House to-day, the court would Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
not be very much influenced by it, but would still have to construe the law, the contract and the terms of this Bill. I do not know that any lawyer in the House would be quite so cocksure on that point as the Minister of Finance is. I doubt very much whether or not the argument might not be made that these commissioners, being merely agents of the government, when they import materials for the government, which will have to be paid for by the government, would not come within the meaning of the statute to which the hon. gentleman has referred. I can well believe that a very fair argument might be made on that point, and therefore I think my hon. friend the Minister of Finance is mistaken when he attaches no importance to the point raised.
I regret that my hon. ifriend represents me as saying that the point is of no importance.
I beg my hon. friend's pardon. That is what 1 understood.

I said, on the contrary, that it might be a question of importance, but it was not the question I was discussing. I was discussing the main question which, I understood, was brought before the House by my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Osier)-not the question he brought before us to-day, but a question of greater importance which he brought before us some days ago. I am in the judgment of the House when I say that the question brought before the House by the hon. gentleman was not the legal question or any question with regard to the adjustment of the capital account of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway some years hence, but the live, actual question as to whether or not these goods were to pay duty. My hon. friend did not say it as a matter of doubt, but he said positively that these goods would not be liable to duty. He is no better authority for that than I am for the counter statement, for we are both laymen, and I fancy that we are both advised. In expressing the opinion I did, I am not expressing my own view alone, but that of good lawyers, whose advice I have taken. What I wish to emphasize is the distinction between the industrial and the legal question brought up to-day. I do not say that the legal question is not important. On the contrary, I say that the question whether or not the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway shall pay interest on the money which the government itself has received by way of duty may be an important one ; but the real question brought up by the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Osier), and which he emphasized, and to which he managed to attract the attention of the country, was the assertion that, under this contract, goods would be imported free of duty and the manufacturers of Canada

would not have any advantage from the tariff. He never dreamt at that moment about the adjustment of the capital account live years hence, but confined himself to the industrial question. The only answer is that the government do not so understand it, and that they are advised by competent legal authorities that such is not the meaning of the contract.
Has my hon. friend any opinion on the question that materials imported by these commissioners would be subject to the duties ?
That is the opinion of the Minister of Justice, who sits behind me.
I did not so understand it.
There is no such provision in the contract.

There is no provision in this contract that the goods shall not pay duty. Will the hon. gentleman show me a line which says they shall not ? He will find no such statement in the contract. All the legislation is the very opposite. The contractors on this Grand Trunk Pacific Railway will be precisely in the same position as the contractors on any other government work. I repeat that I am not dwelling on the legal question, but it does not follow' that I do not attach importance to it, because I do ; and, so far as we have gone at present, we are acting on legal advice. But that is not the question on which the discussion arose, and I leave it to be settled by others. What I confine myself to is the industrial question, and the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Osier) has
not and will not obtain the opinion of any lawyer that these goods must be admitted free of duty.

I think that my non. friend the Minister of Finance is getting himself and his colleagues deeper and deeper into the mire every time he speaks on the subject. Assuming that the government are only able to charge the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway for the net amount they have to pay, how will the thing work out f Take one instance. Take the $20,000,000 rolling stock, the duty on which would be $4,000,000 or $5,000,000. If the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway have not to pay interest on the duty, but only on the net price, they will be able to buy in the lowest market. What will they do ? They will buy their materials in Great Britain, Germany or the States, wherever they are cheapest, and would make the government commissioners contract for them. But assuming that they would pay the duty on these goods, they w'ould buy an engine for $16,000 in the States, which would cost in Canada $20,000, and the government would have to refund the Grand Trunk Railway the amount paid in duty. Or the amount on which the government could charge the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway interest would be the net amount at which they could get the engine without paying duty. The government would have got the duty it is true, but would have to refund it, or, what amounts to the same thing, would not get interest on it, and would have absolutely prohibited the Canadian manufacturer from having any chance to tender. According to the interpretation of the Finance Minister, the government would have to pajt the duty. They would receive with the one hand and give out with the other. They would receive the duties on the materials imported and refund them to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. In other words, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway would only be bound to pay interest upon the lowest cost at which these materials could be brought into the country. The question whether, the government pay the duty has nothing to do with the point. But the manufacturers would be in a much worse position. It would, be a much more drastic measure than I supposed it would be, assuming that the stuff would be imported without the payment of duties.
I am afraid I shall have to follow the opinion of the Deputy Minister of Justice, that I cannot conceive how any hon. gentleman can reach such a conclusion.
But the hon. Finance Minister admits that the Grand Trunk Company will have to pay the interest on the cost, say of the locomotives-
I have never admitted anything of the sort.
I must be very obtuse, then.
Hear, bear.
Or the Minister of Finance has very little capacity for expressing himself. Will he tell us what the object of this clause is ?
It has been explained.
I have not heard the explanation, except that the Grand Trunk Company have to pay the interest on the cost of construction on the eastern division, less the amount of duty.
That is not the way we understand it.

I would ask the leader of the House (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) if the object of this Committee is merely to criticise this contract ? Or is the object in some way to improve the contract 1 Is it the intention of the government that this discussion shall serve a useful purpose or is it merely critical and destined to have no effect ? Can the contract be improved by discussion in this Committee ?
The contract cannot be improved, but the Bill can be improved, if there is a fault in it.

Well, what is the objection to a declaration in a Bill intended to provide for the building of a national transcontinental railway, that national policy shall clearly obtain throughout the contract ? What is the objection to the amendment offered. by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier), which has the effect of so declaring ? Why should we not say that, in the making of the National Transcontinental Railway, Canadian industries, Canadian workmen, and Canadian capital, shall not get the worst of it ? The hon. member for West Toronto pointed out-and this has not been answered-that the materials may be imported by the contractor and duty paid, but that the contractor will then file a claim for the refund of the duty. In that case, Canadian manufacturers and the Canadian workmen have no protection, as they ought to have. The day has come when the people of Canada, whether Liberals or Conservatives, will insist that if this National Transcontinental road is built, it shall be built of material produced in Canada and by Canadian labour. In other words, the people of Canada are in favour of national policy, and they are in favour of it being embodied in a contract of this kind. What is the objection to that ? What is the objection to our improving legislation in that direction ? Surely it is worthy of consideration. The minister has not answered the questions that have been raised here to-day. He said that the goods shall pay duty. But the hon. member for West Toronto says that Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
the importer can claim a refund. That is a question of law. I put two questions to the hon. Minister of Finance. He has answered what he calls the industrial question, but he has not answered the legal question. That question remains, and we have heard the opinions of eminent lawyers read here to-day. And my only objection to them is that they give the Grand Trunk Company a reason for asking for a refund, and the companies will probably ask for it. What is the objection, if we are a deliberate body, and trying to improve this contract, to including in this contract a declaration of national policy ? The people of Canada regret very much that occasion was not taken, when the Canadian Pacific Railway was built, to insist on this rule being applied, and every rail used on that road being rolled in this country. I regret still more that it is not made a condition of this contract.
Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) permit me to ask him a question ? Could he inform the House why the party with which he is associated, in 1867, refused to put a duty on steel rails ?

I have no objection to answering that question. I regret that my party did not put on that duty. I have always been in favour of putting on such a duty on steel rails. We know what made the United States more than anything else
Let us keep to the contract.
Yes, and I want the right hon. gentleman to include national policy in this contract.
It is big enough.

But it does not contain this provision. If there is anything the people of Canada would like to see-and I am speaking strictly to the point-it would be the idea of national policy included in this contract. For, as I said before, a mistake was made in the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway, in not including in the contract a provision that the rails should be rolled in this country. There is no reason why such a provision should not be embodied in this contract. The thing that made the United States more than anything else is national policy with regard to iron. It has put that country at the head of the iron-producing countries of the world. And we shall never be an iron-producing country unless we insist upon national policy with regard to iron manufactures, and especially in relation to contracts of this kind. This is not. as has been said, merely a contract for $15,000,000. This road will cost nearer $200,000,000.
Better say $560,000,000.
It may be that. Speaking about the cost of this railway-
Let us keep to the contract.
The Postmaster General has interrupted me, and I am dealing with the point he referred to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Though an lion, member may interrupt, that does not justify the hon. member who is interrupted in departing from the question.

But there is this to be said, Mr. Chairman-that if there are to be interruptions on certain subjects and no answer is allowed, there is a remedy in the hands of lion, gentlemen on this side, as you, Mr. Chairman, know.

I am quite in order in discussing the cost of this work in connection with this clause. Hon. gentlemen opposite have spoken as if the interest to be paid by Canada represented the whole amount of Canada's obligation in this matter. If a man goes to the bank and borrows $100 and then goes and tells one of his creditors that he only owes $5, the interest on the amount he has borrowed, what will his creditor say when he applies for further credit ? He will say : Your commitment is for $100, not for $5. The commitment in this case on the part of Canada is for the whole cost of the road. The name of Canada is put on the note of the Grand Trunk Company for millions and millions, to build this road. So, when the hon. Postmaster General sneers at an estimate of four or five hundred millions as the cost of this road, I say that we have a better right to estimate it at that amount than he has to estimate it at thirteen or fourteen millions.

I was not giving my own opinion, but the opinion given, as I understood, by the leading financier on the other side. I understood that the junior member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) estimated the cost of this road at $560,000,000. In my interruption, I was only commenting on that, for everybody knows that that statement is an absurd one.

Nobody knows more about investments than the hon. Postmaster General. I suppose nobody in this House has handled more trust funds than the hon. gentleman has handled in his day. And if anyone came to him for a loan and then said that his only commitment to the estates the hon. gentleman handled was the interest on the loan, what would the hon.-gentleman say ? The point before the Chair is the amendment of the hon. member for West Toronto in favour of a declaration of national policy in this contract. If we are here to improve the contract-and I hope we are-surely this would be an improvement.
I hope that a suggestion from this side of the House is worthy of consideration.
Sometimes.

I hope the right hon. gentleman will consider it, and will even let this clause stand in order to make a provision against this very thing that the hon. member for West Toronto has pointed out. The goods can be imported, the duty-can be paid, so that a person paying the duty may hope to have the money refunded. In that case Canadian industries, Canadian mills and Canadian workmen are discriminated against in a way that even the government say they have no desire to do.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance made a lengthy argument in the interests of the industrial classes. Now, if he wants to improve the condition of the industries of Canada let him carry out the idea that was conveyed to the House by the statement made by the Prime Minister when he first introduced this Bill. He left the impression upon my mind, and I think upon the minds of every one who heard him, that all the supplies required for the construction of this railroad would be purchased in Canada. But when the Bill comes down we find that clause 37 of the contract removes that impression altogether. It reads :
The company shall purchase all material anil supplies required for the- construction of the -western division and the equipment of the whole of the said line of railway from Canadian producers

Now, if it stopped there, the argument of the Minister of Finance would mean something, that he is looking after the interests of Canadian industries. I see no reason why that section should not be amended so as to strike out the balance. The balance of the section reads :
-when the same are produced in Canada

Now, there is not an article that will go into the construction of that road, but is produced in Canada, and can be produced, not only in sufficient quantities, but in quantities to afford competition. Therefore, strike out the balance of that clause which reads :
-when the same are produced in Canada, and when such material and supplies can he purchased in desired quantities and of equal quality suitable for the purpose desired, and for prices and upon terms equally advantageous with those procurable elsewhere.
Now, what benefit is that to the manufacturers of this country ? We have heard the legal opinions as to the meaning of this clause, that have been read to the House to-day, and I am prepared to make this statement :	Let the government through
their commissioners, advertise the sections of this road for tender. Let us say that a party is successful in getting a contract to build a section of that road, and to supply
[DOT] 11351

rails and everything else necessary to equip it completely. When he has secured his contract from the government to build that piece of road, he puts an advertisement in the newspapers of Canada, the United States and Germany, for so many tons of rails, spikes, plates, bridge material and all supplies required for the section he has contracted for. The Canadian tenderer will put in a tender, assuming that this contractor will have to pay duty on the goods that he purchases in a foreign country. Now, I am prepared to say that if 1 am a contractor, for example, I cam go to the United States manufacturer and get his prices for every article, and I will be able to compete with those prices at which they are sold in his own country. But he will deliver them duty free, or take his chances in law of getting the duty back under this Bill now before parliament. He can say to the contractor, I will furnish all supplies at the prices iin my own country, and deliver them there duty paid, because I have the assurance from the Canadian-government conveyed in this Bill. This United States manufacturer says, I will pay the duty and I will sue the Canadian government and get it back. And you can go to every foreign manufacturer in face of that contract, in face of the legal opinions that have been produced here to-day, and get contractors to furnish supplies and lay them down here duty paid, knowing that the contractor of the railroad is working for the government, and in such case the law says that when these goods are imported for a government work they will come in free of duty. Now, there is no court in the world but what will decide that these goods were for the government, therefore, they were not dutiable, and the American contractor who supplied the raw material can bring his action against the government of Canada, or the Customs Department, for having illegally collected this money, and he will get it back again. But even if he had not paid the duty, he will be putting his goods into Canada in competition with our Canadian manufacturers. The statement of the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Osier) is quite correct, not a steel rail will be made in Canada for the next fifty years if this clause is allowed to go through as it is, because we will have English, German and United States manufacturers putting goods in at such prices that no Canadian manufacturer will be able to compete with. I say if the government wish to make provision for the manufacturers of this country, let them strike out of clause 37 all the words after ' from Canadian purchasers,' and compel the contractor, whoever he is, to buy all his supplies in Canada. In that way we will do something for the manufacturers of this country, and we will encourage them instead of giving them a blank eye" Here we say to the contractor, yon cannot go on and tender, and buy yotir goods wherever Mr. TAYLOR.
you can buy the cheapest, and we will leave it a question which can be fought out afterwards in the courts as to whether we shall pay the duty or not. All we have today is the statement of the Minister of Finance that the contractor will have to pay the duty when he imports the goods, but if the law says you collected the duty illegally, it will be refunded, so that the manufacturer will have to take his chance on the legal construction of this clause now before the House.

I am wondering if these are the same gentlemen who held up the House all yesterday in the fear that this road was going to be over-capitalized and that freight rates could not be reduced because of the over-capitalization that was going to be permitted. Are these the same gentlemen, I say, who had that terrible fear all day yesterday, and who to-day are holding up the House, insisting that there shall be an over-capitalization in consequence of which the freight rates cannot be reduced '! If the expenditure that the building of this road will entail, and the legitimate opportunities that will thereby accrue to our manufacturers, are not sufficient for them, I am one to say that that is evidence of the necessity of some provision in this resolution that they shall not be able to take this country by the throat and make the treasury disgorge at their own will and pleasure. Whatever will increase the cost of the construction of the eastern section will certainly increase the carrying charges over that railroad. While I, as a citizen of Canada, am anxious to see our manufacturing industries develop and advance, I am also anxious to see those who require to transport their products over this road get an equal chance to live. This road. I understand, is being built for the benefit of the manufacturers as well as for the benefit of the farmers. To enable the manufacturers of eastern Canada to reach their natural market in western Canada, and that can only be done by providing a road at the cheapest cost of construction, which will allow the lowest rates of carriage. I say it would be a cut-throat policy for the manufacturers themselves to do anything to increase the cost of construction of this eastern section, and thereby tend to debar themselves from entrance into and access to their natural and legitimate market in western Canada. If this road has a reason for construction at all, it is to enable the manufacturers and commerce of eastern Canada to get the benefit of the trade of western Canada, and the only way that earn be done is by keeping down the cost of construction so that the government, having control of rates, can keep them down accordingly. I say that while we wish to assist the manufacturers, while we would be pleased to see the manufacturers get all they cam out of an expenditure of $100,000,000, or as some
t

people say, of $200,000,000 or even of $500,000,000, we cannot afford to allow these very worthy gentlemen the power to take the country by the throat aind unduly and inimitably increase the cost of this road as it would be if the supplies necessary for the construction of it could only be bought in Canada. It is no secret that the manufacturers of Canada constitute a huge combine not in one or two limes but in all lines. It would be a piece of idiocy to put the carrying through of any such tremendous enterprise at the mercy of such an organization ; which is apparently the object to be attained by the amendment which has been proposed on the other side of the House.

In answer to the hon. gentleman who is just, I cannot say, about to take his seat, I would say that even if this side of the House had held up the debate yesterday, as to which statement I do not agree, still, after listening to his observations with care, I have come to the conclusion that perhaps we would be justified if we held up the House for some little time further until at least some members obtained even a faint glimmering of the question which is before the Committee. When we find an hon. gentleman from whom one would expect better things, placing himself on record, as he has done this afternoon, as being utterly unable to vote for the amendment, fighting a windmill which does not exist, protesting against an amendment which would compel all supplies to be bought in Canada, an amendment which is not before the Committee at all, but which would be rather ridiculing the gold brick in the clause which would be presumed to mean that all supplies would be bought in Canada, and when we find him condemning a certain line of policy which would justify the collection of customs duties on the materials used-because, as he very properly said, if customs duties are collected on the materials used in the construction of the road the cost would be increased, the carrying charges would be heavier and therefore he protests against customs duties being collected-surely, when he took such a position as that, he had not listened to the utterances of the hon. Minister of Finance.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Northrup) would make a more intelligent speech if he had listened to what I said.

I listened very attentively to what the hon. gentleman said. It was not very profound. There was no great difficulty in following it, and it was easier to follow it since nothing like it had been heard for some time past. If the hon. gentleman will take the trouble to read the amendment before the House, he will find that the amendment merely asks the government to have it in black and white in the contract so that there may be no possibility
of doubt about it as to what the intention of the contract is. It seems a pity that we should have a long discussion upon a point upon which apparently both sides of the House are agreed. In the opinion of the hon. Minister of Finance the government will collect these duties. We do not think they have power to collect these duties under the contract, and this amendment is brought forward by the hon. member for West Toronto, and if it is carried it is then practically certain that the government will be able to do what apparently they wish to do, but what nearly half of the members in this House think they will be unable to do. If I might for a moment refer to the remarks made by the hon. Minister of Finance, I would venture to say that he has not wholly understood the exact position in which the opposition stand with reference to this amendment. He spoke of the distinction between the industrial question and the legal question, and there can be no question as to what he meant. But, I would call his attention to the fact that while there is an industrial question as to the payment of the cash as duties, the question is not as to who is or who is not to pay tliege duties based upon a legal question. Until that legal question is solved conclusively nobody can speak with certainty upon the industrial question. That can only be a matter of opinion. If the legal question were settled conclusively there could be no question as to the working out of the industrial question. We entirely dissent from the parallel used by the hon. Minister of Finance, that the contractors under this Bill would be in the same position as the contractors for any other government work at the present time being carried on. He referred to lighthouse and other contractors. We are quite prepared to say that if the government makes a contract with any contractor to build a lighthouse, unless there is something in the contract relieving him from the necessity of paying customs' duties, it is perfectly clear that he must pay the customs duties. So far both sides of the House will be in agreement. But, that is not the case before the Committee at the present time. We have a contract which has already been signed between the government and a corporation. One of the terms of the contract according to the fifth clause is that :
The said eastern division shall be constructed by, and at the expense of the government.
Certain obligations will then result from that contract which has been made between the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and the government, subject, of course, to the approval of parliament. When this contract was made the contract itself did not provide, because it was not necessary, that articles imported for the use of the government should be admitted free of duty. The tariff provides, by article 450. that ar-1 tides imported for the use of the govern-

ment, or of any department thereof come in free of duty. When the Grand Trunk Pacific entered into this contract with the government they did it knowing the law of the land. They bound the government to build a railway, and the law was that all materials that the government used would come in free. It is perfectly true that in this Bill the government provides for the manner in which it is to carry out this contract with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. It first provides by clause 2, that the schedule is approved and ratified, and it provides for the carrying out of the contract, only varying as to matters of detail, the procedure in carrying out the contract already made, and thereby ratifying the contract, providing that certain commissioners to be appointed are to do certain work, that these commissioners are authorized to employ certain contractors to do the work that the government has agreed to do, and the government knew at the time they made this contract that nothing we could pass in this House would at all alter the respective positions of the parties. If. the government having made the contract, we by a- vote of this House were to change that contract, tlie other party would be absolved. The contract would be at an end. I presume the intention of the government is to see that the contract is carried out as they have made it. Well then, if that be their intention let us see how it would work out. The hon. Minister of Finance says : I took down his exact words :	We say all goods
must pay duty. We say as a matter of obligation that we will see that they do pay duty. An obligation by whom and on whom? Would you say to the contractors : We are going to collect the duties. But the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company may say to the government :	We dare you to
collect the duty. Bet us see how it may work out in practical life. If the government has to build 1,400 miles of road from Moncton to Winnipeg, and if the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company contemporaneously has to build another line 1,800 miles long from Winnipeg to the coast, the construction of these two roads is provided for in the agreement. If the government is bound to do a certain thing by that agreement, if by the government failing to carry out that agreement any loss is imposed on the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, they will be entitled to damages. If. as a matter of fact, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway has bound the government that it shall not collect the duties, if then the government does collect duties, even if paid by a third party, and if damage has resulted to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company it will be entitled to a remedy as against the government. If thousands and thousands of tons of rails are to be purchased in the old country by the government for its end of the line, and if thousands and thousands of tons of rails are to be pur-Mr. NORTHRUP.
chased by the Grand Trunk Pacific Company for its end of the line, anything that will promote business in those lines, anything that will cause a demand for rails and that will lower the price is in the interest of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company as well as the government. Therefore, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company may say : One of the objects we had was to compel you to get your rails in Great Britain or the United States. We knowing that the greater demand there would be, the cheaper would be the price for us, and therefore the more money we would make out of it.
It seems to me that under the clause of the contract allowing a reference to arbitration, we would not have to wait for the expiration of ten years before the legal .question, which the Minister of Finance wishes to avert, would of necessity arise. Immediately on the commencement of the construction of the road and the letting of the contracts, the question of the payment of customs .duties by* the contractors .for the eastern division (would arise. The 47th clause of the contract reads :
Any dispute which may arise as to the meaning or construction of this agreement, or as to the performance of any of the obligations of either of the parties to this agreement, or as to working expenditure or cost of construction, shall, if not herein otherwise provided for, be determined by the aw'ard of a single arbitrator, if the parties concur in his appointment, or if not, by the award of three arbitrators, one of whom shall be appointed by the government, one by the company, and the third, by the tw* so appointed, or, in the case of their being unable to agree, by the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada, and the award of a majority of such three arbitrators, shall te final.
There is a clear clause, that at any time during the currency of this contract, if any dispute should arise, a reference may be made to a single arbitrator ; and under this clause one individual would have it in his power-an individual outside of the Minister of Finance or the members of the government-to decide whether or not, under the terms of this contract, the government has the right to collect duties from contractors bringing in these materials. No one in this House would hesitate to take the word of the Minister of Finance ; we have not the slightest doubt in the world that it [DOT] is bis intention to collect these duties when he says it is bis intention to do so. But if, on looking at the contract, -we see that there is a clause by which the matter can be referred to arbitration and the award of the arbitrators is made final, we may well believe that the Minister of Finance may have to come down to parliament a few years later on and say : I intended to collect these duties ; I think they ought to be collected, but unfortunately, under the terms of the contract, the power has been taken out of my hands ; I must apologize, and you can-

not blame me for not doing what I am powerless to do. We are endeavouring to shield the Minister of Finance from that danger. We would avoid any such undesirable consummation, and inasmuch as he wishes to collect these duties, we suggest that this amendment would so strengthen his hands that there can be no doubt of his power to collect them.
A word as to the position of the House generally upon a question of this kind. I can well understand the embarrassment of a lay member of the House when a question. such as this Is, wholly dependent on the legal construction of a document ; I can understand a layman saying : I do not understand this, I must take some one's opinion, and I prefer to take the opinion of the Minister of Justice. I have no fault to find with any member of the House who has such respect for the opinion of the Minister of Justice that he feels justified in following it. There are gentlemen on this side oif the House who, like gentlemen on the other side, are ready to profess sincere respect for the opinion of the Minister of Justice on any legal question. But I am sure the Minister of Justice himself would not claim to be infallible, and the very fact that so many members-perhaps the majority-are personally unable to decide this legal question, and are basing their vote on his judgment, should make the Minister of Justice, if possible, doubly careful to be absolutely certain that there is not even the possibility of mistake in the opinion he has reached. The opinion of the Minister of Justice has .been fortified by the opinion of . the Deputy Minister of Justice, and the deputy minister is a gentleman whose legal qualifications we, on this side of the House, are as ready to admit as are hon. gentlemen opposite. But any one can see at a glance that, without belittling the opinion of the minister and his deputy, when we come to weigh the combined opinion of the jegjal gentlemen op the other 'side1, the opinion of the minister and his deputy does not stand on the same footing as if these two gentlemen occupied different positions, and without consultation had arrived at the same conclusion. One gentleman is the head of the department ; the other is his deputy. The Minister of Justice must have gone to his deputy to secure his opinion, either before the minister announced his own opinion or afterwards. If the Minister of Justice had gone to his deputy before he announced his own opinion, it is rather an embarrassing position for the Minister of .Justice, who naturally would not say that he went to his deputy because he was afraid of his own opinion. The minister must have gone with his own mind made up on the question.
I am not at all above admitting that I am not infallible in law. I have enough experience to prevent me from assuming that

But the Minister of Justice is head of the department, and the deputy minister is his deputy, and wre can quite see that if before this opinion was given the minister went to his deputy, it would be a difficult matter for the deputy to lay down his views as being opposed to the views of his chief:	If, on the other hand,
the minister went to the deputy after he announced his own opinion to the public, I think every one will see that the deputy minister would hardly feel justified in setting up his own opinion against that of his chief, and especially such a very eminent chief as is the present Minister of Justice.
Mr. McCarthy. Surely the hon. gentleman (Mr. Northrup) would not say that it was the duty of the Deputy Minister of Justice to follow the opinion of his chief, and that if he differed from the opinion of his minister he should write out his opinion in the same trend as that of the- minister ?

I hope the hon. gentleman tMr. McCarthy) has not misunderstood me. I would be very sorry indeed to think that the Deputy Minister of Justice would express an opinion in which he did not concur, in order to please his chief. Not a word I have said can be open to any such construction. I am pointing out that there is a difference between the Minister of Justice going to his deputy to get an opinion and the opinion of two independent gentlemen .in different cities, arrived at without communication. Surely, every member of the House can see that there is a difference, be it great or be it less, between the position of the two opinions. When we have the opinion of two legal gentlemen, one living in Toronto and another, one of the most eminent members of the Montreal bar ; surely there is enough to justify us in saying that the government have not made their Bill so perfectly clear that they can be certain it will attain the end they have in view. We apparently agree as to the end desired, and why not make it beyond peradventure that what both sides of. the House profess to desire shall be carried out in this contract ?
flow, Sir, a word with reference to Mr. Heilmuth. The Minister of Justice referred to this gentleman, I will not say in contemptuous terms, but he referred to him as having been a foeman whom he had met in the Supreme Court but a short time ago, and the Minister of Justice referred us to the records of the Supreme Court to see the result of Mr. Hellmuth's deliberation and argument and display of ability before the court. The impression was left on members of the House that it was nothing but an act of good-natured generosity on the part of the Minister of Justice that prevented him saying, in so many words, that lie had beaten the learned counsel from Toronto to a finish in the Supreme Court of this

country. I have always found it wise to take the advice of the Minister of Justice when I can, and my only regret is that I cannot take it oftener than 1 do. And so, the Minister of Justice having advised us to look at the records of the Supreme Court, I took the trouble to see if there was anything on that record which would justify us in holding Mr. Hellmuth in less esteem in consequence of the decision of that court, or in believing that we should attribute to his opinion less weight than his high reputation in the country demands we should attach to it. In searching the records of the court I found, as a matter of fact, that there was an appeal by the Calgary and Ed-Imonton Railway against the Grown. I found, also, that the counsel for the appellant was Mr. Hellmuth, of the city of Toronto, and that the respondent's counsel was the learned Minister of Justice. And I saw, Sir, that no doubt it was a feather in the cap of Mr. Hellmuth that he was even pitted against so distinguished a lawyer as the Minister of Justice. When I came to look at the record and the result, I found that Mr. Hellmuth was appellant in a case in which there was a judgment adverse to his side in the court below. Under these circumstances he appeared before four judges of the Supreme Court of Canada. Mr. Hellmuth did not win the case, it is true, but he won two judges out of the four, and the only reason he did not win was because there happened to ibe an even number of judges, and, under the constitution of the Supreme Court, that equal division of opinion amongst the learned judges confirmed the decision of the court below. When a counsel, pitted against the Minister of Justice, appears before four judges of the Supreme Court of Canada as counsel for appellant in a case which was lost in the lower court, and when he can succeed in persuading two out of the four Supreme Court judges that he is right, and when the only reason he did not succeed was because there was an even division of opinion on the Supreme Court bench ; when a learned counsel lias succeeded in doing so much, it is some little tribute to his success. I do not think that the learned Minister of Justice will continue to insist that there was anything in connection with that case which should lower the general opinion held of Mr. Hellmuth. And then, Sir, curious to see who it was of the four judges of the Supreme Court that Mr. Hellmuth succeeded in convincing, I found that they were the learned Chief Justice- and I am sure everybody on cither side of the House is proud of the ability and erudition which the learned judge has brought to the bench-and Mr. Justice Girouard, while the Minister of Justice succeeded in holding the late Mr. Justice Armour and his late colleague. Mr. Justice Davies ; so that Mr. Hellmuth was unable to secure what was necessary to reverse the first judgment. I only mention Mr. NORTHRUP.
this, because I concluded, from the reference made by the hon. Minister of Justice before lunch, that Mr. Hellmuth suffered a most ignominious defeat, worse than Waterloo, in the Supreme Court; and I wished to make the descent of the hon. gentleman into Hades as gentle as possible. I was satisfied that in any case, outside of political questions, it was wise to accept the legal opinion of the Minister of Justice. I have no doubt that the Minister of Justice shares the view of his colleague, the Minister of Finance, because it is incredible that two members of the administration should hold different views on this question. I hope he will accept the amendment of the hon. member for West Toronto, because it simply puts into plain language the views which the Minister of Finance has announced as the views of the government.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Would the.hon. gentleman read the section in the Customs Act which declares that all goods purchased for the government shall come in free, and give it to the hon. leader of the opposition before he asks for his opinion ?

Both the hon. Minister of Justice and the hon. Minister of Finance, on different occasions, have clearly stated that it was not the intention that the materials used for the construction of the eastern division of this railway should come in free of duty. But, as has been pointed out, a legal interpretation of the Bill and the contract is contrary to their views in that respect. The Minister of Finance, I am inclined to think, did not take from the opinions which the hon. member for West Toronto read to the House the meaning which they conveyed. He stated that there were two questions-the industrial question and the question of the company paying 3 per cent interest upon the total cost o<* the. eastern division, which the government are to build; that when the hon. member for West Toronto spoke a few days ago on this question, he referred to the industrial question only; and that the legal opinions which he has read have reference solely to the question of the payment of the 3 per cent interest. I am bound to believe that when

tlie lion.
