Minister of Finance reads these opinions, as they will be found in ' Hansard,' he will have reason to change his mind in regard to that, because my understanding, and I think the understanding of most of the members of this House, is that the provisions set forth in the Bill and the agreement mean that these goods will have to come in free of duty. I am a layman like the lion. Minister of Customs, and do not pretend to give my view on these questions. But, according to my limited knowledge of the matter, if the government constructed this road, they would not pay duties, because they would be simply taking money out of one pocket and putting it into another; if the government delegate their powers to a commission, I am inclined to think the commission will not have to pay duties ; and if the commission delegate their powers to men who construct the railway by day's work or to contractors, they will not have to pay duties. This is an important matter to the working people of this country. I would have gone further than the hon. Minister of Finance. If our credit is sufficient' to enable us to raise $100,000,000 to build, this railway, surely the time has come when the ordinary cars and locomotives, and everything used in the building and equipment of the road, should be made in this country. I am prepared to admit that we have not at present the facilities in this country to make, in a short space of time, all the locomotives, cars and other articles required for this railway. But what X do say is that the very fact that we can go abroad and borrow $100,000,000 or $120,000,000, a considerable portion of which will go into the handis of alien workingmen in foreign countries. is evidence that the time has come when we should look this question fairly and squarely in the face; and, Instead of putting in this Bill a clause like section 17, I would be inclined to go as far as to provide that the equipment and everything required for this railway should be made in this country. The hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) took a peculiar stand in reference to this matter. I would like to say to that hon. gentleman that I believe the time is coming when he will be glad to have car shops in Edmonton, and when the people in the great cities of the North-west, which are bound to rise in the future, will be glad to have every thing required for this railway made in the Northwest. All the people of that country are not going to till the soil. Among the thousands and tens of thousands of people who will go into that country, a great many will not want to till the soil, but will flock into the centres of population; and the time is coming when the towns and cities in the North-west, in the natural course of things, will need to have industries; and I would be inclined to make it obligatory that the rolling stock for this road should be made | 356
in this country. If this clause is meaningless to some extent, as I understand hon. gentlemen claim that it is, why is it there? It must be there for something. Was it the clever lawyers of the Grand Trunk Kailway that got it put in or those responsible for the drafting on behalf of the government? Somebody must be responsible for it; and if the Minister of Customs and the Minister of Finance want all doubt removed, they will consent to the amendment. We believe that the time has come when we should not vote money to be spent in foreign countries.

With reference to section 37 and the contention that the company should be compelled to purchase all its materials in Canada, without any qualification whatever, it is obvious that such a condition would be impracticable. It might retard the completion or the equipment of the road for years. It is well known that all the locomotive works we have in this country are now engaged up to their full capacity. It is impossible for them to meet all demands, and many leading railway companies have had to go to the United States, England and Germany for their locomotives. But suppose you were to put in a clause compelling this company to purchase everything in Canada without any qualifications, and business were to go on increasing as I think it will, it might be impossible for the company to get in Canada, within any reasonable time, the equipment it will require. When I addressed the House some days ago, I alluded to the fact that one-half the materials might be purchased in this country and the other half might be imported and furnish a revenue. We thus secure to the Canadian manufacturer the protection afforded by the tariff.
What we want is to get the goods manufactured here.
Our manufacturers will get the full benefit of the tariff.
But they do not get the work.
They will get all they can do and they will have an advantage of $35 dollars in the hundred over the Americans. If they can sell their goods at $35 over the American price, they will get the orders.
The whole discussion has been why there should be any ' if ' at all. Why not make it so plain that there will not be any ' if ' about it.
Will the hon. minister tell us exactly what clause 17 of the agreement does mean ?

I have said that I am a layman and I am giving my view of section 37. If the Grand Trunk



Pacific Railway import any of its material, it will have to pay the duty, and that duty will be a protection for the Canadian manufacturer. It is very probable that, with the rapid construction of the road and increasing business, they will not be able to get all the equipment they want in Canada and they will have to import some. In such a case, they will have to pay the duty ; and if the Canadian manufacturers sell all they can make and the country is getting a revenue from the balance, I cannot see why any one should complain. As we have had the opinion of the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Osier) and the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) on section 37, would the hon. the leader of the opposition have any objection to stating whether, in his opinion, under clause 37. the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway will not have to pay duty on the materials they import.

I think that my hon. friend the Minister of Customs has enough on his mind in connection with section 17, which he does not seem to understand very well, to justify him in confining his attention to that section. Let me assist him in coming to an understanding of clause 17 first, and then we will come to clause 37. What is the purpose of section 17, lie-cause that is the one that is prior in the Bill and with which the opinion of the Minister of Justice, which I have before me, is concerned. Perhaps the Minister of Customs, who understood the matters very well, will give his view of the purpose and object of section 17.

I have been very courteous with my hon. friend, and I think I am justified in insisting that he should give me the information I ask. The reason I ask it is because the hon. members for Toronto and Leeds say that all the materials mentioned in clause 37 will come in free, and I would like to have the legal opinion of the hon. gentleman as to whether there is anything in that contention. My own opinion as to section 17 would not be a legal opinion. My hon. friend knows my view with reference to the industrial question, but I think it is germane to the discussion and only fair that he should give us his opinion on section 37.
Why is clause 17 there ?

Since my hon. friend the Minister of Customs, cannot be persuaded to give us the slightest information as to the purpose of clause 17, I propose in the first place to endeavour to enlighten him with regard to that clause. It is really the clause with which we are concerned in the matter we are discussing. It is the clause which is dealt with in the amendment of my hon. friend from West Toronto and is properly considered in the opinions read by the hon. member for West Toronto, and the opinion of the Minister of Justice which I have before me. The

Minister of Finance states that section 17 is put there for some wise purpose, but up to the present, neither he nor any other minister of the Crown, with the exception of the Minister of Justice, has given any suggestion whatever as to the reason why it is inserted in the contract.
I have looked over the opinion of the Minister of Justice, an opinion of course which commands every respect and which is commendable because it puts before the House in very clear terms the view which he entertains of the legal question we are now discussing. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice in the first place recites clauses 16 and 17, he does not recite clause 15, which I think has an important bearing upon the matter, though he refers to it later on. He says that clause 15 of the contract defines the expression ' cost of construction.' He says that the expression ' cost of construction ' means and includes all the cost of material, supplies, wages and many other things ; and he says :
Clauses 16 and 17 provide for additions to the cost of the construction. It is imperative under the Bill that-the work of construction of the eastern section shall he by contract, and the Bill does not enable the government to import or pay for materials to be used in construction.
The Minister of Justice takes that ground, but I am unable to concur with him. Then he continues as follows :
These, as I understand the Bill (section 15), are to be furnished by the contractor.
My hon. friend makes no argument with regard to that, he simply states it as a bald conclusion. But he hinges everything upon that, because his further conclusion is as follows :-
Consequently clauses 16 and 17 of the contract can have no application to original construction.
Well, he does not seem to me to have given sufficient weight to the expressions used in clauses 15 and 16. In clause 15 you have the expression ' cost of construction ' defined, and that cost of construction applies to construction In the first instance. Clause 16 applies to the expenditure after a lease has been taken of the eastern division, and it uses an entirely different expression. Clause 16 is as follows :
In case, after the completion of the said eastern division and the taking possession thereof by the company under the lease thereof, hereinafter referred to, or at any time thereafter during the continuance of the said lease, the government shall deem It necessary to expend any sums of money for the improvement of the said eastern division, the replacement of structures by others more modern, or otherwise upon capital account for betterments, and not being ' working expenditure ' payable by the company, the government may expend such sums, and the amount thereof shall be added to the capital of the construction account.
Now, here you have two expressions contrasted with each other. The words ' cost

of construction ' In clause 15 are applicable to construction In tlie first instance before tfie lease, and tbe words ' capital of tbe construction account ' are used in respect of the expenditure made by the government after the lease. Then when you come to clause 17 you find both these expressions used, obviously for a purpose.
No addition shall be made to the cost of construction or to the capital of construction account.
The very expression which is defined, if I may say so, in section 16. Therefore, you have the two expressions well defined, one, the cost of construction, relating to original construction, and the interpretation of which is to be found in clause 15 ; and tbe other expression, 1 the capital of the construction account ' the meaning of which is defined in clause 16. But you have both these expressions referred to in clause 17, the all important clause to which attention is being directed. It does not seem to me for these reasons that I could concur in the conclusion of the Minister of Justice that clause 17 is not sufficiently comprehensive to include not only additions to construction after the lease comes into operation, but also the cost of construction in the first instance. My bon. friend's opinion seems to depend upon that consideration, and upon this further consideration, that he thinks he finds somewhere in this Bill that which would prevent the government from importing material for purposes of construction. Well, I hardly think we can find anything in this Bill to lead to that conclusion. The Minister of Justice bases his conclusion upon the terms of section 16 of the Bill which we are now considering. That section provides that the commissioners shall let the work of construction after the plans and specifications thereof shall have been duly advertised, and they shall accept the lowest tender. Suppose you have this road graded and ready for laying the rails, is there really anything in section 16 to prevent the government, or the commissioners acting for the government, from importing these rails and then letting by tender the work of putting them in place ? I do not find anything in section 16 which leads to any such conclusion, and for that reason andi with all respect I would not be inclined to concur in the opinion of the Minister of Justice in that regard.

In view of the statement made by the leader of the opposition with respect to this section, I think it is the part of prudence, so far as I am concerned, to ask that the section be allowed to stand so that I may further consider it. In making this suggestion, I think I ought to refer to what has fallen from my hon. friend from East Hastings (Mr. Northrup). In what I said this morning, I thought I had been careful not to say anything that might be considered disrespectful of the legal gentleman to whom he referred and 356J
for whom I entertain tbe highest regard ; but I have looked over the ' Hansard ' report of what I said, and I fear my language was, to say the least, unfortunate, and calculated to convey a wrong impression. I wish to repeat what I said before, that I had no intention of saying anything disrespectful of Mr. Hellmuth, of whoni I entertain the highest opinion because of his great reputation at the bar. I want to add in that connection, that I was mistaken, perhaps, and conveyed a wrong impression this morning with respect to the result of the appeal. The appeal to the Privy Council in the case of the Calgary and Edmonton Railway is still pending.
Might I ask the Minister of Justice if, in his opinion, the supplies which go into the betterment of tbe road shall come in free of duty ?

If these supplies which go into the betterment of the road are imported directly by tbe government, then of course they would come in free of duty. If they were imported directly by the government, and not through any contractor, and to be used by the government for the construction of the road, in that event they would fall under the general terms of the Customs Act which has been in force in this country since 1886, and would come in free of duty. But if these goods are imported by a contractor in connection with the construction of the eastern division, or imported by the Grand Trunk Pacific in connection with the western division, it was the undoubted intention of tbe parties that these goods shall certainly pay duty, and that that duty shall be added to the cost of construction upon which the Grand Trunk Pacific are to pay 3 per cent. That was the undoubted intention of the parties- to this agreement, and of course it is our duty to see that that intention is made so absolutely clear that there can be no possible doubt about it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: There must be some reason why that clause was put in the contract. What'is the reason that clause 17 was put in there ?

If the government, after the road is constructed, and has been handed over under lease to the Grand Trunk Pacific, required to have certain improvements or betterments made as provided in section 16, and if the government imported these goods directly, if clause 17 were not in the contract, notwithstanding that the importation was made directly by the government, it would have been possible for the government to add them to the cost of construction and to make the Grand Trunk Pacific pay interest thereupon.
Not under the Customs Act, would it ?
Yes. I "will read the Customs Act.
What is the use ?
It is of use.
It will not convince anybody.	[DOT]

I do not know whether it would convince anybody or not, but I want to satisfy myself. Section 5 of the Customs Act provides :
Subieot to the same provisions and to the further conditions contained in schedule B to this Act, all goods enumerated in this schedule B may be imported into Canada or may be taken out of warehouse for consumption in Canada without the payment of any duties of customs thereon.
Then, article 50 of schedule B reads as follows :
Articles imported by or for the use of the Dominion government, or of any of the departments thereof, or by and for the Senate or House of Commons, including the following articles when imported by the said government or through any of the departments thereof for the use of the Canadian militia: military clothing, musical instruments for military bands, military stores and munitions of war.
That is the clause in force at the present time. It is that if the government imported these goods direct they would come in under the operation of schedule B, clause 450, and would not he liable to customs duties. That is the law which has been In force since 1886.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It is not necessary that the government should import them direct. It says 'by and for,' and therefore these goods could be imported1 by the contractor for the government.
"it is useless to argue the question.
I understand that under this clause the government are allowed to bring in these articles free of customs duties ?	[DOT]
Yes, but not in connection with the construction of this road.
Any articles used by the government could be brought in free?

If the the government by day's labour and if the government imported the articles that were used by the government in the construction of the road these articles would be imported free of duty. Section 16 of the Bill is intended to prevent that, because it says that the government cannot construct the road, but that it must be constructed by a contractor. Then, it will be dealt with absolutely in the same way as the construc-Mr. HUGHES (Victoria).
tion of canals, and canals are being constructed in this country every day. Contracts are given for the construction of canals. The contractors import the goods and when they do so they pay the duty.

In view of the legal opinions which have been given and considering the bargain with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, this certainly does not look like an ordinary contract. We have the opinions of these gentlemen given very straightly that they think the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company are bound to bring in these goods free of duty. The liou. Minister of Finance says that they mean to collect the duty.

I cau go a little further even than my iron, friend the Minister of Justice did and I will take a case where government to-day have the right to import materials without passing them through the customs. The fact is that in the Department of Railways and Canals we do not avail ourselves of that privilege when the goods are produced in Canada. When tenders are invited from people in Canada the rule of the Department of Railways and Canals is that these tenders shall quote the duty-paid price; so that the government do not avail themselves of the privilege where the goods can be got in Canada of importing direct.
If the government ac-i cept that position why not put it in the contract ?

That might be necessary if we were considering the old Canadian Pacific Railway contract, as there was a difficulty of that kind in connection with that. There is none in this. The conditions here are entirely different.

Apparently a distinction is drawn by the government between the work to he done in the first construction of the road and the work to be done subsequently. The intention apparently is that imported materials going into the first construction of the road shall pay duty and that imported materials going into the later improvements or betterments shall not pay duty.
If the importation is made directly by the government-with that qualification.
Why do the government draw the distinction and why do they make that provision ?
Because the general Customs Act which has been in force since 1886 makes that distinction; because it is the law of the land to-day.

Then, apparently the hon. Minister of Justice does not understand that the law is being interfered with, kept in abeyance as far as the first construction

of the road is concerned, but is allowed to go into operation as far as subsequent betterments are concerned.

Not at all. The first construction must be carried on by the interposition of the contractor, the goods must be imported by the contractor, and if imported by the contractor they would not come within the provisions of section 17, which apply to goods directly imported by the government. The words,
' directly imported,' are in the clause.
Could not subsequent work done upon that road be done by a contractor ?
Then, the goods would not be directly imported by tlie government and would pay duty.

If after the work of construction is completed the case arose that was mentioned by the hon. leader of the opposition that the government should undertake to bring into the country a large quantity of rails and rolling stock, which would not be done through a contractor, wouldi they not come in free of duty ?
Then the government would deal with those rails as they deal with them on the Intercolonial Railway, and have dealt with them on the Intercolonial Railway for years past.
In what way is that ?
They do not pay any duty on them.
Then, the contention of my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Osier) is sustained and supported by the hon. Minister of Justice.
That is my hon. friend's view, and he is entitled to it.

The hon. Minister of Justice sustains that view. He has said that in that case the same course would be followed as is followed by the government today, and that they would import these goods free of duty.

If there is direct importation of rails for the Intercolonial Railway by the government for the use of the government on the Intercolonial Railway .these rails come in free. If it is in connection with a contract let upon the Intercolonial Railway for the purpose of construction that an importation is made, then the contractor will have to pay the duty. That is the distinction.

The result of it is that after the work of construction on the eastern division is done if the government choose to import rails directly they will import them free of duty. That is exactly the same position that the hon. member for West Toronto is trying to guard against. The whole purpose of his amendment is to secure for the manufacturers and rolling mills of Canada the production of these rails, and apparently the hon. Minister of Justice has admitted that the provision that my hon. friend wishes to introduce must be introduced or else the government would be in a position to import these rails frtee of duty.

There is nothing which says that even for the first construction the goods shall not pay duty. It says that if you see fit to import rails for later betterment and duty is levied thereon, then the duty shall not be charged up to capital account, but there is nothing to prevent the government buying the rails in Canada if they wish to do so.
Or from buying them abroad if they wish to do so?

Certainly, the government must be perfectly free to buy them wherever they please. If the government buy the rails in Canada, then there is no question of duty in the matter at all. If the government see fit to bring these rails from abroad then they cannot charge the duty on these rails to capital account of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, in the account for the betterments on the road. But there is nothing even then which obliges the government to import the rails at all. They can purchase them at home, and there is no question of duty entering into the matter.

I did think some time ago that I understood the purpose of clause 17, but I am now beginning to doubt whether I have a correct realization of it. It is really very peculiar, as I think the hon. Minister of Justice will admit. Clause 17 says that:
No addition shall be made to the cost of construction or to the capital of construction account in respeot of customs duties In cases where there is direct importation of material or supplies by the government.
For the purpose of what I am going to say I will take the view of the hon. Minister of Justice as to the object of this clause. Let us assume that he is right and that I am absolutely wrong. What purpose does this clause fulfil after all ? If goods are imported directly by the government they must come in free under the provisions of the Customs Act which has been read by the hon. Minister of Justice. Then, under clause 16 you cannot charge customs duties to the Grand Trunk Pacific because it would be excluded by the very terms of clause 16. What does section 17 do ?

As the law is now, any importation of material by the government under section 16 would

come in free of duty, and of course in that case there could he no addition to the cost of construction or to capital account for customs duties. But this contract has been made for fifty years, and the law as we have it now with respect to the importation of materials by the government may be changed next year, or at ainy time, but with respect to this particular contract it will remain as it is to-day.
The sole purpose of it then is to provide against the possibility of customs duties being charged some time in the future upon direct importations for the government.

That is my opinion.

On section 19,

This clause prevents any member of either House of parliament from being appointed to any position of emolument under the commissioners, or from being a contractor or party to any contract with the commissioners for the construction of the eastern division. It is a very desirable clause so far as it goes, but has the government considered the desirability of having it go a little further ? From what was said by the Finance Minister to-day we would understand that the office of commissioner will be an office of emolument, and the clause does not say that no member of either House shall be appointed to be a commissioner.
No member or senator could hold am office of emolument under the Independence of Parliament Act.
Not if he were to retain his seat in parliament.
It is not contemplated that he should be a commissioner and retain his seat in parliament.

I had in mind as to whether the government considered the advisability of saying that no member of the Senate or House of Commons should be appointed to the office of commissioner, even at the risk of being compelled to resign his seat.
The Postmaster General formerly contended that no member or senator should he appointed to office until a year after he had resigned his seat.
I can frankly say that we have no member of parliament in view at all. If he were appointed he would have to resign his seat, and my hon. friend (Mr. Borden) would-not

speechtext: ask more than that even if some suggestions were made in former times that a year should elapse.

The Minister of Finance is putting it very mildly when lie calls it a suggestion. My recollection is that there was a motion made, accompanied by a very strong speech from a gentleman who is now a very prominent member of the cabinet. It would seem as if the reasons which were so forcibly advanced only a year before this government came to power, should be equally cogent with the ministers to-day. Has the Prime Minister had recent occasion to consider these statements which were formerly made by his Postmaster General. Perhaps the opinion then held by the Postmaster General and his present colleagues has not been entirely dissipated.

I agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Borden) that no member of parliament should be a member of this commission, and there is no intention that he should be. There is no provision in this Bill to prevent the appointment of a member of parliament, but the Independence of Parliament Act would immediately apply and the member appointed would at once have to vacate his seat. It seems to me that in this respect the clause goes far enough. Does my hon. friend think there is any doubt that a member of parliament cannot be a member of this commission ?

I thought that) the Prime Minister might have been so far impressed by the speeches of the Postmaster General, as to conclude that it would be unwise to appoint a member of parliament until one year after he had ceased being a member of this House. A very Tiigh authority in the government has advocated that principle, and although we may not all agree with it, yet in view of the fact that it was so forcibly presented to the House by so able and distinguished a minister, I thought that the government might have considered it, and arrived at a matured and well considered decision with regard to it.
I agree with my hon. friend that it is advisable for the government to take that into consideration," and arrive at some mature decision upon it.
There is nothing in this clause to prevent a senator or a member of the House of Commons being a shareholder or a director of a construction company to build this road.
I am afraid that is right.

If there is nothing to prevent either a member of the House of Commons or a senator being a member of a construction company, and as the independence of Parliament Act precludes the

possibility of a member of either of these branches of the legislature being a contractor, what is the necessity for this clause at all ? Would not the Independence of Parliament Act preclude either a senator or a member of the House of Commons being a contractor ?
Yes, inevitably.
As they may be members of a construction company, why not eliminate the clause altogether ? It is simply surplusage.

This provision is applicable to a contract taken from these commissioners, and it was adopted word for word from section 19, of the Intercolonial Railway Act. In the Independence of Parliament Act a member of a company which has a contract is exempted from the application of the Act.
That is all very well ; but the Independence of Parliament Act precludes a senator or a member from being a contractor.

This clause is necessary, because the contract would be made with the commissioners, and not with the government directly, and therefore it would not come under the operation of the Independence of Parliament Act.
The commissioners are acting [DOT] under the government, and they would have to be treated as one and the same.
If the clause were struck out, members of parliament could take contracts from the commissioners.
Does the Minister of Justice hold that view ?

It is open to that. The object of the clause, I take it, is to place a member of parliament in exactly the same relation to the commissioners as he holds to the government. If there is any doubt about that, this clause makes it absolutely certain.

Under this clause all that is required is for several senators or members of the House of Commons to unite themselves together in a construction company, to enable them to take contracts from these commissioners.
That is the case to-day.

Another clause pi'ovides that the contracts must be ratified by the government. So that the government will have the farming out of all the contracts, and will be able to brush aside the commissioners, and let every contract to construction companies composed of senators and members of the House of Commons.
My hon. friend is not aware that section 15, of the Independence of Parliament Act permits that very thing to-day.

Under the present law, I understand that any member of either of the legislative branches may be a member of a joint stock company which has a contract with the government; if that is not correct, the Auditor General's Report proves that the Act is being violated, because I need not refer to a certain senator who is connected with a company whose name figures prominently in the Auditor General's Report for supplies furnished. Surely the hon. Minister of Justice does not contend that members of the Senate or House of Commons should be able to combine themselves into a construction company to take contracts under this Act.

The difficulty about the present situation is that the sud-posed safeguards for preserving the independence of parliament are more apparent than real. Any member of parliament or senator can practically make himself a corporation by associating with himself four other people, giving each of them one share, while he holds, let us say, the remaining 996 shares, thus making himself practically as much interested in contracts bet,ween that corporation and the government, as he would be if he made the contract himself. Yet there is no doubt, as the Minister of Justice observed, that that is a perfectly legitimate transaction, a transaction which cannot be attacked under the law as it exists at present ; and the consideration of that subject in connection with the section which we are now discussing, opens up a pretty wide range. If it is desirable to preserve the independence of parliament-and I do not think any of us can have any doubt in regard to that-is it not a serious question for the consideration of this House whether some amendment should not be made in the present law ? I do not minimize the difficulties of dealing with the situation ; because I have put an extreme case. You might have a case quite as extreme the other way. You might find a member of parliament interested to a minimum extent in a company which has a contract with the government. Still, it seems to me that parliament should give some consideration to the question, either in connection with this clause or in connection with the Independence of Parliament Act. Half a dozen members of this House might form themselves into a construction company, and be vitally interested in contracts virtually made with the Crown, and the Act relating to the independence of parliament would not permit us to criticise their action in that regard in the slightest degree.

This question is not new. I remember it being discussed

In he early eighties at some length, when the same difficulties were suggested as have presented themselves to the minds of my hon. friends to-day. X am sorry to say that no satisfactory solution has yet been found. I remember when in 1878 several seats were vacated on the most trifling offences. Some members of parliament were members of printing companies, and because there had been a government contract taken by a company for three or four dollars, thejy were deprived of their seats. We had a case somewhat similar this year, in which the hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Schell) was concerned, and we can easily imagine cases in which the independence of parliament might be violated unconsciously. I remember that the best solution devised was that when a member of parliament was also a member of an incorporated company, the fact that he held shares in such a company and that it had a contract with the government would not be a violation of the Independence of Parliament Act. He did (not contract individually, but simply in his corporate capacity. But the law is very likely to be abused, and some abuses were brought to the attention of parliament some time afterwards. A firm, for instance, might take out letters of incorporation and practically all the stock be held by one man who was a member of parliament. There was no satisfactory remedy, but in the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway it was decided specifically that no member of parliament could be a member of the corporation except under specific circumstances. This is a public work, and the law could be applied that no member of parliament can be interested in a corporation that has anything to do with public works.

The view taken by my right hon. leader is no doubt correct. The general principle of the law is that no member of the House of Commons can be interested in any government contract. Section 15 of chapter 11 of the Revised Statutes says :
This Act shall not extend ho disqualify any person as a member of'the House of Commons by reason of his being shareholder in any iu-oorporated company having ,a contract or agreement with the government of Canada.
If the law stopped there, It would be perfectly clear, but the statute goes on to provide an exception :
Except any company which underbakes a contract for the building of any public work.
I think that in view of section 8 of the Bill, which provides that [DOT].
The eastern division of the said Transcon-ential Railway extending from the city of Moncton to the city of 'Winnipeg, shall be constructed by or for the government in the manner hereinafter provided.
That provision of the Bill makes this a public work within the meaning of section 15 of chapter 11 of the Revised Statutes. Therefore no member of parliament can be Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
interested in a 113' contract under this Bill, even as a member of an incorporated company. That Is my view at first sight, but it is a serious matter, and I would like to hear how far hon. gentlemen opposite share that view.

It would be a little difficult to speak off-hand on a provision of the statute. There is one suggestion I would like to make in connection with the observations of the Prime Minister. The situation is a little different to-day from what it was in the early eighties. The tendency during the last ten years has been to put everything into the shape of a corporation. Business enterprises, which were conducted in the form of a partnership twenty years ago, are now incorporated. Men are incorporating themselves because by doing so they escape some of the contingencies which beset the ordinary partnerships. For instance, their liability is limited to the amount of capital invested by them. Therefore the evils, which were apparent in the early eighties with respect to contracts between the government and corporations are very much greater at present. I suppose that nine-tenths of the great commercial business houses of the country are now conducted in the shape of corporations, whereas fifteen or twenty years ago they were ordinary partnerships. The illustration to which the Prime Minister has adverted indicates how slight a difference there is between the two cases. One of the cases, I think, was in Nova Scotia. Certain gentlemen had associated themselves in a partnership, but bad not taken the precaution of filing articles of Incorporation and were held to be disqualified on account of some printing contract with the government, whereas if they had gone through the form of filing articles of incorporation, not the slightest question could have been raised. In 1880 no further legislation was thought necessary, but the conditions were somewhat changed to-day. and it might be desirable for the government to consider whether or not-although I see the difficulty of it-some advance might not be made in our legislation in that regard.

Before the discussion closes, I would like to ask for a few words of information. I do not know that I have followed correctly the position taken by the leader of the opposition and the hon. member for Simcoe. But I understand that they take the position if any member of the Senate is interested in any ^enterprise of this country, that enterprise shall thereby be prevented from doing any business with a contractor or the commissioners who are to be intrusted with the building of the eastern section. I would like to know whether that is the position taken by these hon. gentlemen ?
Mr, BENNETT. As far as I am concerned, I wish to have it publicly under-

stood, by an expression of opinion from the government, that senators and members of parliament may combine themselves into a construction company, particularly under view of clause 15 which reads to this effect:
Provided always that no contract under this section involving an expenditure of ten thousand dollars or upwards shall be concluded by the said commissioners until it has been sanctioned by the Governor in Council.
In other words, every contract on this work will be at the will of the government, because there will be no contract under $10,000, and they are practically going to settle who shall have the contracts. If It is to prevail that senators and members of the House of Commons combine in a company, the friends of the government may be able to make contracts with the government.

It is not to prevail. It is not the law now that senators and members of the House of Commons can form an Incorporated company to take a contract for the construction of the eastern division ; and in order to make the matter perfectly clear, if the hon. gentlemen will read section 15 of chapter 11 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, he will see that no member of parliament can be a member of an incorporated company, if that company takes a contract for the construction of public works. This would be a public work in the meaning of that section.
Would that apply to the case of a member of parliament furnishing rails or rolling stock.
That would come within the meaning of that section.
Furnishing mere materials or supplies would hardly come under the heading of a public work.

The supplies are for a public work. I understood the hon. gentleman to refer to a corporation furnishing supplies for this particular enterprise. Then it would be a contractor for a public work.
Section 19 allowed to stand.
On section 20-salaries of commissioners and employees,
I wish to move an amendment to that clause, to strike out the words ' in the first instance,' at the end of the first line.
Has the government considered the names of the persons whom they are to appoint as commissioners ?
They have not.
No one in sight at all ?
Not yet.
We have strong hopes we may be able to find somebody.
It is ail important matter, and the government should consider the appointment of these commissioners.
Let us consider the Bill first.
Yes, I suppose that is important, too.
The amendment of the Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) leaves it to the Governor in Council to determine absolutely tlie salaries of tlie commissioners at all times ?
Yes.

Would it not be proper for the government, as they are asking parliament to entrust this power to them, to give some idea of what the proposed commission will cost and what the compensation of the members is likely to be fixed at ?

On section 21,
The Governor in Council shall have the power at any time to suspend the progress of the work on the said eastern division until the then next session of parliament.
This is a very important section on the face of it. I think it would be desirable that we should have some explanation of it before the committee is asked to pass it.

This is taken from another Act of a somewhat similar character. The Minister of Justice informs me that it is the Intercolonial Act. It is simply a general power to suspend the operations of the commissioners, if, at any time it may be found necessary. There is no special transaction in mind-this is simply a reserve power in the hands of the government to properly supervise the whole work.

When the construction is suspended, there is no responsibility on the part of the Grand Trunk Pacific to carry out the patriotic proposal of shipping grain over Canadian lines and through Canadian ports. If the construction of this line is suspended, the Grand Trunk will be free to ship western grain by Chicago, Duluth and New York.
They are going to do it any way.

There is a difference between this case and that of the Intercolonial. In the case of the Intercolonial, there was no contract with a company for the building of the road, it was a matter which the government had entirely in its own hands ; it was building for itself, it might suspend operations when it pleased. But here you have contracted to build this road ; and you have no clause in that contract to suspend operations, alliough you are putting it in this Bill. Has the Minister of Justice considered what will be the effect of the suspension ?
It is only a suspension between two sessions of parliament. We do not attach such importance to it that we want to struggle for the clause.
That might mean a year or nine months.
I wish there were a year between sessions, but unfortunately we cannot count on that.

This might involve the country in liability to the contracting company in the case of suspension of the work. One provision of this contract is that the Dominion shall construct this eastern division. The Grand Trunk is building the western division in the expectation, they will say, of making an enormous sum of money by running their traffic over the eastern division. If you suspend operations for nine months, no doubt the Grand Trunk would point to the language used in this House to sustain their contention-that they have sustained enormous loss by not having this valuable road under their control.

We do not attach great importance to the clause, except as it assures governmental and parliamentary control. As I say, we have nothing special in view ; this clause is only to keep the country on the safe side.

Has the hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker) read section 22 ? Under that section, the work cannot be carried on, unless there is money available, and there cannot be money available unless there is a parliamentary appropriation. If the appropriation became exhausted, it might be useful to have statutory power to suspend the work.

My observation applies to that section also. It is in the Bill, but not in the contract. You are agreeing in the contract to carry on a certain work, and then you take the power, in the Bill, to suspend the work. Should not these provisions be inserted in the contract ?
There is no time limit within which we are to provide the road.

But the contract is that you are to go on with reasonable despatch ; and a deliberate refusal on the part of parliament to make, or the government to ask for, appropriations would hardly be consistent with your contract. I do not say we object to this clause, but I do say it should be accompanied by some provision that the exercise of the power under this clause shall not subject the Dominion of Canada to damages.
I would ask the Minister of Justice-it will be useful information- whether refusal or neglect on the part of Ministers of the Crown to take an appropriation ever gives rise to damages ?
This clause is to be found in all the contracts of the Department of Public Works.
That is the point I am raising ;-this provision is not in the contract, but it is in the Bill.

But there is no contract, so far as the construction of the eastern division is concerned, beyond this, that we are to supply the road, after const ruction, to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. There is no provision in the contract with respect to the construction itself.

But the contract implies that you are to go on with reasonable despatch with the construction of that road. And, if you suspend operations deliberately for six or nine months, that is not going on reasonably.
Unless you have good reason for the suspension.

I do not know that that would be an answer to your contract. Here you are making a contract, and then in an Act of parliament you are enacting a clause by which parliament authorizes the government to suspend the work-in other words, authorizing you to impair your contract. Now, the question is whether, when putting in that clause you should not have protection against liability.

I cannot see that there is any question of liability. But I may say this clause was drawn with, the express purpose of reserving absolute parliamentary control over this work, and it seems to me it forms part of the clause that follows after, which makes provision that no payment shall be made until after a parliamentary appropriation has been made for it. I am not entirely committed to this clause, but I thought it would be wise and in the public interest to reserve absolute parliamentary control over the eastern division.

1 think they are prudent clauses, hut you want something more, you want a provision in this Bill that will bind the Grand Trunk Pacific so that they cannot claim damages against you for exercising control under the provisions of this Act. *

For example, it occurs to. me at the moment that a difficulty' might arise in this respect:	There is no
doubt this is a contract between two parties, and I would think that in the absence of parliamentary appropriations or otherwise, there would be a claim for damages, if any damages could he proved upon a breach of that contract. The contract says that the parties contract and agree with each other that, according to clause 5, the said eastern division shall be constructed ; and according to clause 8, that:
The construction of the said eastern division shall be commenced so soon as the government has made the surveys and plans and determined upon the location thereof, and shall be completed with all reasonable despatch.
Then assuming you have once commenced the construction of the road, and this section 21 implies that the work has begun, you might have a claim for damages from the Grand Trunk Pacific. Suppose they had provided $5,000,000 worth of rolling stock, but owing to the default of the government in not proceeding with the work with reasonable despatch, that rolling stock became useless and remained on the hands of the company for a considerable time-there might be then a legitimate claim for damages. The difficulty witfi regard to the clause is, it seems to me, that while it gives the Governor in Council power to suspend the progress of the work, there is no corresponding clause in the contract such as is usually found, that the suspension of the work by the government shall not be the foundation of any claim for damages at the suit of the other party.

That would be a proper clause in a contract between the commissioners and a contractor. But I cannot see how it would he possible in the construction of the eastern division, with which, of course, the Grand Trunk Pacific has nothing to do.

I may be wrong, hut I will lay before the Minister of Justice the way that clause presents itself to me. The clause to which I have referred is a very usual one as between the government andi the contractors. The government usually embodies a stipulation in a contract that it may suspend operations upon the work, and that such suspension shall not involve a claim for damages. The Minister of Jus-tive truly says that this would be a proper clause in n contract between the commissioners and a contractor. But would it not also be a proper clause in this contract itself, for the reason I mentioned a moment ago ? Suppose the Grand Trunk Pacific Company made provision for the operation of this road, suppose it made provision under the terms of the proposed lease for rolling stock and many other things which involve the expenditure of money. Well, the government suspend operations, and cannot the Grand Trunk Pacific Company go into court and file a petition of right against the government, and say :	Yon have not
proceeded with this road with reasonable despatch-because you have acted upon a clause which is not a part of this contract at all, a clause in the Bill affirming this Act, it is true, but which does not in that respect modify the terms of the contract between the company and the government- and for this reason we are entitled to claim against the government such damages as have accrued to us by reason of the delay. That may be improbable, but it is certainly possible, in view of the contract and the terms of the Bill.

Under the operation of the clause, might not the government, if they saw fit, drop the eastern section entirely ? Might they not, if they wished, drop any other part of the scheme, or any part of the section which this Bill deals with ?
But we have no intention of doing that.

If, after the government have made surveys and found out that the mountains of information did not materialize, and that they would not he justified in going on with this road, would not this section give them an opportunity of getting out of it ?

I was going to make that very point. Could not the government and the Grand Trunk Pacific, by connivance, from time to time suspend the operation of work on this eastern section so that it will never be built, and thus the patriotic policy will never be carried out ? Now this provision may be for the purpose of enabling the government and the company, by connivance, to suspend the construction of the road. Therefore there is no guarantee in the Bill that the patriotic portion of the contract is really to be carried out.

It would appear as if this would allow a considerable amount of latitude to the government in dealing with the construction of the eastern portion of the road. This applies to the whole road from Winnipeg to Moncton, and if at any time the government is disposed to suspend the progress of the work upon the eastern division, does this imply that they can suspend the work upon the whole of the eastern division ? It is to be presumed that the government would commence the work at different points, for example, from the west

ern terminus at Winnipeg, and at Moncton, and perhaps at three or four intermediate points. Now suppose under this provision the government suspended the work upon one part of this road and continued it upon another. They might, for instance, continue it upon the western portion of the road and not continue it upon the eastern portion. For instance, they might start work at Winnipeg, and working towards North Bay, they might go on with that portion of the road which would give the Grand Trunk Pacific a connection with its Grand Trunk system in Ontario; because if that work were completed from Winnipeg to North Bay or the neighbourhood, and a branch were constructed from North Bay to the main line north of North Bay, then that portion of the eastern division might go on to completion, giving the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk their connection with the Grand Trunk system in Ontario, and with the ports of Montreal and Portland. But it must not be forgotten that a large part of the promise made in this Bill is to the people of the province of Quebec and to the people of the maritime provinces. The Bill is so drafted as to hold out the prospect of a large amount of railway extension and construction throughout, not only the province of Ontario, but through'Quebec and through New Brunswick. Now it would almost seem possible that the government might use such a clause as that introduced here to proceed with the work in such a manner as best to suit their own interests as a government, or perhaps the interests of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company ; they might suspend work on any portion of the eastern division, because they are expressly empowered at any time to suspend the progress of the work upon the said eastern division. According to that language. I would suppose they could suspend the work upon one part of the eastern division, but not upon others. They might in that way carry on the work in such a manner as to disappoint to a large extent the anticipations of the people of Quebec and of New Brunswick. If the government really have not very much faith in the possibility of carrying grain from Winnipeg to Quebec over this new road, if they have a doubt, a doubt in which I would be inclined to share, (they might suspend indefinitely the construction of the eastern division. It would scarcely seem to have been made clear to tills House that with the water competition with which that road would have to compete it would overcome the difficulty, and there might be some necessity for delaying the construction of the eastern part of the work. The government, by this section, are providing an easement of a very extensive character. Then again, I think the members of the government might explain what is entirely meant by the language of the section. It says that:

That the Governor in Council shall have the power at any time to suspend the progress of the work upon the said eastern division until the then next session of parliament.
Does that imply that immediately the next session of parliament is convened the work must be resumed or is it intended to mean that the government are to be allowed to suspend the operation of the work because they require to get a new authority from parliament or require the advice of parliament in reference to some difficulty that may have arisen, or that they require the intervention of parliament to supply them with funds which are to be expended undersection 22 of the Bill which provides that no money shaM be paid until sufficient appropriation has been made by parliament for that purpose ? The language of the section is not very illuminating, it does not give a great deal of light, and reading it in the form in which it appears in the Bill, it would seem to give the power of suspension of the work until the next session of parliament is convened. It may be that the suspension may continue not only until the next session of parliament is convened but until any date that may occur during the next session of parliament, or possibly the suspension may continue until the end of the next session of parliament. I do not see anything objectionable in the clause because it gives the government power to suspend the work in a case where it might be of national importance that the work should be suspended. There might be some question of great urgency in our national affairs, some great national distress, or something which would make it important that the work should be suspended, but I think it would be well if the lion. Minister of Justice would inform us as to what is the exact intention and to what extent the government would use the provisions of this section.

This Is a clause that seems very clearly to confer upon the government a discretionary power which is to be exercised subject to the control of parliament. All it provides is that the work may be suspended until the next session of parliament. Then the matter is in the hands of parliament to be disposed of by parliament. It seems very clear, especially if we look at section 22 which makes special provision for the appropriation and which says that no work can be done in connection with this enterprise unless provision is made by parliament for the payment of the work to be done. The intention of both sections 21 and 22 is to reserve the matter to the control of parliament so that parliament may have absolute control over the whole work.

Is it amply understood that iu case such power is used and the work is suspended under the authority of this section and the matter submitted to parlia-

ment at the next session what the position of this public work would be ? Would it be submitted to parliament for further authorization to proceed with the work and for further aid ?

May I draw the attention of the hon. Minister of Justice to another point ? Suppose the Grand Trunk Pacific Kailway, having constructed their line from Winnipeg to the west, having completed it within five years, find that the government have not possibly more than commenced the construction of the eastern section of the line, they would, of course, be compelled at the outset and during the very first year to find an outlet other than the eastern division for their freight. Suppose they find that the government have been slow in the construction of the eastern division, as I would suppose it will not be constructed for ten or fifteen years, they will run a line following the red line indicated on the government map as far as Winnipeg, then, having already their line to Duluth and Minneapolis, all they have to do is to get a connecting link from Winnipeg to Duluth and they have a through line to the sea. If the Grand Trunk Pacific establish the route by way of Duluth they will have a vested right. In case the "government delay the construction of the eastern division would it be possible for the Grand Trunk Railway Company to make an excuse that they have a grievance against the government and refuse to carry out then-part of the contract in relation to traversing the eastern division when it is completed ? I do not think that any mam who understands anything about business considers that the Grand Trunk Railway have any intention of running one car over this eastern division. I think they would be very foolish to do so. Therefore, would it not be well to make provision against any excuse whereby the Grand Trunk'Pacific Railway Company could advance ainy plausible reason why they should not carry out their part of the contract to operate the eastern division of the system ?

I am afraid there is only one remedy that I can suggest to meet such a condition of affairs. If, at the end of five years, which is the time mentioned for the western section to be completed, we find as my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes, Victoria) suggests, that the government are just about beginning the eastern section of the road, all we can do is to get rid of that government very quickly and get another government into power.

There is another and a more serious difficulty from the maritime point of view. This matter should not be thrown into politics every year and that is the object of this section 21. Why should the building of the eastern division be thrown into the legislative wrangle every
year 1 If this is a national railway there ought to be no provision in regard to coming to parliament about it every year. Parliament should be absolutely committed to the building of the eastern section us an inter-oceanic transcontinental line and there should be no question about the matter being brought before parliament every year. The only question that should be brought before parliament is the question of providing the funds. We should be absolutely committed to the building of the eastern section. The eastern section is more important than the western section. The Atlantic seaports are more important. No country is worth a cent that is not a maritime country and I believe the eastern section is more important than the western section if you are going to have a transcontinental railway. I am bound to say, however, that I think the location is absolutely fatal. But, parliament having taken a different view, I say that the eastern section should not be made a football from this time out and that there should be no question about parliament having to deal with it beyond the duty of providing the money. Otherwise it would be very easy for the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway to bring on an agitation hereafter. The easiest way the Grand Trunk could devise to defeat this scheme, would be to work up an agitation to get the government to suspend work, and have the whole question thrown into the arena of public debate again. Once we have settled on this scheme, it should be final, and the Minister of Justice should take that section out of the Bill.
Would my hon. friend permit me to ask him a question ?
Any number of them.

I was about to explain how this condition arose. But we in Ontario all know that the judges who hold circuits are given a certain allowance for holding circuits. And, as a matter of fact and of experience, the judges are able to save something by economy, not living as they did in the old days, when every judge who held circuit in a country town gave a bar dinner. By dispensing with' such luxuries, the judges are able to save something out of the circuit allowances. The result is that, if a lawyer takes a position in a high court of justice, he is in receipt of a higher salary than if he were promoted to the Court of Appeal. are in receipt of a higher salary than judges of the higher court. I am sure that no one can advocate that state of affairs. And any person must see that the inevitable result of the present condition of affairs must be that, if our judges in appeal are left in receipt of lower salaries than are given to the judges of the inferior courts, the day will come-I do not pretend to say that it has been reached as yet-when the Court of Appeal will be inferior to the other courts whose judges are better paid.

All round,

distant when it will be necessary for us to take hold of this question seriously. One of the difficulties in connection with the salaries of the judges arises from the fact that while the government and parliament of Canada fix the salaries of the judges, we have no control over the number that may be appointed in the different provinces. I think that difficulty was realized by the Prime Minister years ago when the government of which the late Sir John Thompson was Prime Minister, undertook to introduce a measure increasing the salaries of the judges. If I am not mistaken, the Prime Minister, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the late Hon. David Mills stated, either publicly or privately, that they would not be prepared to sustain the government of the day in that measure.
Not I.

I understood my right hon. friend entertained the view then, that the judges were too numerous for the work which was to be done, and that the Conservative party having control of the number of judges in the province of Quebec at that time, ought to see that that matter was regulated, and that no increase in the number of judges should be asked

for. Of course, if my right hon. friend states that that was uot his view at that time, I accept his statement at once, but I so understood it on the authority of Sir John Thompson himself.
I think my hon. friend will agree with me that there is an anomaly in our constitution at the present time.

That is what I was saying, I commenced my remarks with that observation. If you take the aggregate amount paid for judicial salaries in .Canada at the present time, I am inclined to think it is quite enough to secure us a good bench in all the provinces of Canada. Two additional judges are to he appointed in the province of Ontario. I am not familiar with judicial matters in that province and I do not know how far they may be necessary. But I would be inclined! to consider in connection with that increase the fact that one of the judges of the high court of that province is at present absent from his judicial duties, and is engaged in performing work on a commission in the Yukon. That is not a matter that is easy to deal with and I do not know just what remedy we ought to adopt unless we undertake the task of discriminating in some way and that would be a very difficult task indeed, I know, for this parliament or for any government. Would it not be possible for the government to suggest to the governments of the provinces when they undertake to provide new judges whether or not the appointment is necessary ? The question is one of the anomalies that we have in our constitution and for my part, though I have had occasion to think a good deal over it, I have never been able to satisfy myself as to the remedy which we should adopt unless it be a radical one. I remember very well that when Sir John Thompson was Minister of Justice the matter was brought up and for my part I expressed the opinion then that in the province of Quebec the system of judicature was very unsatisfactory. We have no county court judges in our province. We have only Superior Court judges and I thought that the system which prevails in Ontario would be far more suitable to our province. I do not know if Sir John Thompson communicated at that time with the local government, but, I do know that my hon. friend from Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) who was then attorney general introduced a Bill in the direction of changing our system and introducing the Ontario system. Unfortunately that Bill was defeated and for my part I always regretted it. Since my own friends have been in office in the province of Quebec I have urged repeatedly to try and change their system but they have told me that it is impossible because the opinion of the province is against it. I hope that some day there will be a change in public opinion and that we will have a different system introduced into the province of Que-

bee. But even then the anomaly would still exist if it is in the power of the local legislature to create the courts and fix the number of judges and leave it to the Dominion parliament to provide for the salaries. It goes without saying that there could not be a greater anomaly than this one, because the legislative authority which creates the court should also provide for the payment of the judges. Perhaps we should find some remedy for this condition of things if we could have the system which exists in the United States of having provincial courts and federal courts. If we had provincial courts to administer the laws of the province and federal courts to administer the laws of the Dominion I think it would possibly be a more logical system and perhaps be more useful to the different provinces and to the country as a whole. If we had reason to believe that the thing was done under motives which were not warranted and if it were to be akin to fraud, or something of that kind, then, this parliament would be justified in refusing to act.
